content.content:
### B.2 — Four processes, not one 🔒

`D-002` (corollary) · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

`obdd`, `storaged`, `analyzed` and `supervisor` are separate processes with separate
address spaces, communicating over a shared-memory ring and Unix domain sockets.

**Why.** Fault isolation is the product requirement, not an architectural preference: the
analysis engine is the most complex and least trustworthy component, and it must not be
able to take the capture path down with it. One process would be simpler and would fail
the thing the device exists to do.

### B.3 — The ring refuses rather than overwrites 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Claude, from D-002 · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

When the ring is full the producer returns failure and increments an overrun counter. It
does **not** overwrite the oldest unread slot.

**Why.** Overwriting loses data silently, and silent loss is the exact failure mechanism F
exists to make impossible. A refusal is visible, countable, and reportable; an overwrite
looks like a quiet minute. Enforced by `tests/test_ring.c`.

**Reviewer note.** This is a real trade: under sustained overload we drop *new* data
rather than *old*. If that is ever the wrong choice for a diagnostic, reopen this.

### B.4 — The phone is a read-only window over the device's own Wi-Fi ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-013` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

**Decision.** The Pi runs its own Wi-Fi access point — WPA2, a per-device passphrase, **no
upstream connection, no internet**. The owner's phone joins it and opens a status page
served from `src/interface/` by a supervised child process. The page shows exactly two
things — **status** and **current verdicts** — rendered from the same supervisor UDS verbs
`obdctl` uses. It holds no state, runs no analysis, and writes nothing. `obdctl` remains
the primary, exact interface with all five verbs. No app, no account, no cloud, and the
phone never pairs over Bluetooth. (The Pi itself pairs with the OBD2 adapter, D-019.)

**Why.** The user is a car owner, not someone with a terminal in the passenger seat, so a
product that can only be read over SSH has no user. The handout permits it directly
("Serving a dashboard on the LAN is fine", §3.3; CLAUDE.md §2.1), and the device keeps
working with no phone present at all. It also sharpens the phone-app test: the Pi is the
part that is awake at every key-on; the phone is only a window onto what it already
recorded.

**Why so thin.** The handout warns: *"Resist the pretty web app. A crisp CLI with five
query verbs and exact semantics is more defensible, and far more extensible at the
live-modification station."* So the page is a view, not a second interface: two screens,
no framework, and no number on it that `obdctl` cannot also produce. Every graded behavior
remains demonstrable through `obdctl` alone.

**Cost.**

- A network listener in the product. It binds only to the AP interface, is read-only, and
  lives only in `src/interface/`, where `make boundary` already allows network symbols.
- One more process in the 48-hour RSS plot, and Wi-Fi radio power on the car's USB port.
- The access point shares the Pi 4's one radio chip with the Bluetooth link to the adapter
  (D-019). Measured by `btcoex`.
- **Open sub-decision (M2, both):** the server's language. C in `src/interface/` keeps an
  interpreter out of the memory-stability test; Python in `ui/` is permitted by CLAUDE.md
  §2.5 but adds ~30 MB RSS to the soak. Recommendation: C, because the page is tiny.

### B.5 — One warning light, driven by the supervisor ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-014` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

**Decision.** One LED on a GPIO (proposed GPIO17, header pin 11, through 330 Ω), written
**only by the supervisor**. Every state in which the device is working is a *blink
pattern*:

| Light | Meaning | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| fast blink (~4 Hz) | **degraded** — a child is down, the adapter silent while the engine runs, storage failing, or undervoltage | highest |
| double-blink, pause | **a verdict has surfaced** (after D.3 hysteresis and dwell) — look at the phone | |
| slow blink (~1 Hz) | on duty, recording, nothing to report | lowest |
| **steady on or steady off** | **the device is not running.** Never a valid state. | — |

**Why a light at all.** The 3 a.m. test: nobody is looking at a phone at the moment that
matters. It also makes "honest reporting through our own interface" (demo movement 1)
visible from across the room when a sensor is unplugged.

**Why every live state blinks.** A GPIO keeps its last level after the process driving it
dies. If "verdict" were solid-on, a crashed supervisor would freeze the light into a false
alarm, or into a false all-clear if it froze off. With blink-only states, a stuck light of
either kind can only mean *not running*. This is mechanism E's principle — a recorder that
dies silently has harmed its user — applied to the one output a driver actually sees.

**Why the supervisor, not `analyzed`.** The supervisor already knows every child's
liveness (mechanism E), so it can show "degraded" when `analyzed` itself has died; a light
owned by `analyzed` would show a stale verdict instead. Verdicts reach the supervisor over
the existing UDS. One writer, no GPIO contention.

**Cost.** One more thing the supervisor does, and one more thing it must not block on: the
blink timer must never delay `waitpid` handling. Color, brightness and placement are open
(M4 enclosure).

---

## C. Storage and data integrity

### D.1 — Self-trained model; training in Python, inference in C 🔒

`D-004` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden (confirmed with instructor)
· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

A locally-trained, self-authored model is permitted; hosted APIs and third-party
pretrained weights are not. Therefore: training in `tools/train/`, weights versioned under
`models/` with the training commit in the header, **inference in C in `src/analysis/`**, no
network at runtime.

**Why inference in C.** First and most important for the grade: the runtime path sits
inside the supervised multi-process architecture, and a Python process there muddies the
boundary a grader must verify in sixty seconds. Second: it removes an interpreter, a
garbage collector and ~30 MB of RSS from a 48-hour memory-stability test we are graded on.

**What the model is not doing.** The features are the intelligence — operating-point
binning, per-bin baselines, Mahalanobis residuals, Theil–Sen trends, all hand-written.
Delete the weights file and the system still produces residuals and trends; it loses only
the final labeling step. That separation is deliberate and it is the answer at the defense.

### D.2 — Analysis pipeline shape 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

Operating-point binning (RPM × load × coolant temp) → per-bin running mean/variance →
multivariate residual (Mahalanobis) → robust trend (Theil–Sen) → classifier → state
machine with hysteresis and dwell.

**Why binning comes first.** Comparing a cold idle to a warm cruise is a false-alarm
generator. Every comparison happens inside one bin, against genuinely comparable
conditions. This single step removes more false positives than anything else downstream.

**Why multivariate.** The signal is the *correlation between sensors*, not any single
sensor's value — oil pressure is supposed to rise with RPM. A measure of anomaly that
already accounts for normal partnerships, and alarms only when a partnership breaks, is
what makes this something a threshold provably cannot do (handout §3.3).

### D.3 — Hysteresis and dwell before any verdict surfaces 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

No verdict reaches the user until it has persisted. Trip and un-trip levels differ
deliberately.

**Why.** A monitor that cries wolf twice gets unplugged, and an unplugged monitor is worse
than none because someone far away believes it is on duty. **False-positive rate is a
first-class metric in `docs/EVALUATION.md`, not an afterthought.**

### D.4 — The threshold test, as a standing rule 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

Every diagnostic we ship must require at least two cooperating sensors to reach its
conclusion. If a single threshold on a single value could produce the verdict, it is not
intelligence and it does not count. **Write the reason down in `docs/DESIGN.md` when
adding a diagnostic** — this is checked at the defense.

---

## E. Scope, claims and evaluation

/* Single-producer / single-consumer lock-free ring from capture to storage. It is the
 * handoff mechanism E's process boundary needs, and mechanism F only if a Pi-side sensor
 * gives it a high-rate stream (D-017).
 *
 * The no-drop guarantee is the point. A gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis,
 * so a drop must be impossible to hide: every slot carries a sequence number and the
 * consumer accounts for every one of them. If the ring is full the producer must
 * report the overrun rather than silently overwrite an unread sample (DECISIONS B.3).
 *
 * Layout is fixed so the ring can live in shared memory across the process boundary
 * that mechanism E requires.
 */
#ifndef CARWATCH_RING_H
#define CARWATCH_RING_H

#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#define RING_CAPACITY 4096u   /* power of two — the mask depends on it */
#define RING_PAYLOAD    16u   /* bytes; a Mode 01 reply's data (<= 4 bytes) fits with room */

typedef struct {
    uint64_t seq;                    /* monotonic, never reused */
    uint64_t mono_ns;                /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC at capture */
    uint32_t pid;                    /* (mode << 16) | PID — room for 16-bit Mode 22 PIDs */
    uint8_t  len;
    uint8_t  src;                    /* data_src_t — live | replay | synth */
    uint8_t  _pad[2];
    uint8_t  data[RING_PAYLOAD];
} ring_slot_t;

typedef struct {
    _Atomic uint64_t head;           /* producer writes */
    _Atomic uint64_t tail;           /* consumer writes */
    _Atomic uint64_t overruns;       /* refused pushes — must stay zero */
    uint64_t         _pad[5];        /* keep head/tail off one cache line */
    ring_slot_t      slot[RING_CAPACITY];
} ring_t;

void     ring_init(ring_t *r);

/* Returns false when full. Never overwrites an unread slot; increments overruns. */
bool     ring_push(ring_t *r, const ring_slot_t *in);

/* Returns false when empty. */
bool     ring_pop(ring_t *r, ring_slot_t *out);

uint64_t ring_overruns(const ring_t *r);
size_t   ring_depth(const ring_t *r);

#endif
/* Structured logging. Every line is machine-parseable, because the 48-hour soak log
 * is a graded deliverable and we will have to plot it. (handout §3.4) */
#ifndef CARWATCH_LOG_H
#define CARWATCH_LOG_H

#include <stdint.h>

typedef enum { LOG_DEBUG, LOG_INFO, LOG_WARN, LOG_ERROR, LOG_FATAL } log_level_t;

/* Data provenance. CLAUDE.md §2.7: replayed or synthesized data is labeled as such
 * EVERYWHERE it appears. This field exists from day one so that it is impossible to
 * forget later. */
typedef enum { SRC_LIVE = 0, SRC_REPLAY = 1, SRC_SYNTH = 2 } data_src_t;

void        log_init(const char *component, log_level_t min);
void        log_set_src(data_src_t src);
data_src_t  log_get_src(void);
const char *log_src_name(data_src_t src);

void log_emit(log_level_t lvl, const char *fmt, ...)
    __attribute__((format(printf, 2, 3)));

/* Hourly heartbeat: process liveness, RSS, cumulative event counts. Required by the
 * soak (handout §3.4) and the source of the RSS-vs-time plot in docs/EVALUATION.md §3. */
void log_heartbeat(uint64_t events, uint64_t drops);

#define LOG_D(...) log_emit(LOG_DEBUG, __VA_ARGS__)
#define LOG_I(...) log_emit(LOG_INFO,  __VA_ARGS__)
#define LOG_W(...) log_emit(LOG_WARN,  __VA_ARGS__)
#define LOG_E(...) log_emit(LOG_ERROR, __VA_ARGS__)

#endif
# soak/ — the 48-hour unattended run

The handout requires the logs to show, at minimum:

1. A timestamped startup.
2. A heartbeat **at least hourly** recording process liveness, resident memory (RSS),
   and cumulative event counts.
3. **At least one injected fault** during the run — physically unplug a sensor for ten
   minutes, or `kill -9` a sensor process — with detection, degradation, and recovery
   visible in the log.
4. An orderly state at the end.

Raw, unedited logs are the graded deliverable. **Do not tidy them.** Real systems are
never that tidy, and a cleaned soak log is the artifact this course is best equipped to
notice.

## Before the graded run

Start soak-style overnight runs at small scale from **M3**, not M4. Every leak found in
Week 9 is a crisis avoided in Week 14. `make soakcheck` runs a one-hour miniature.

Leave margin to run the graded soak **twice**. You will want to.

## Open: what the soak runs against

See **D-006**. Until it closes, build as if live sensors are required.
# tools/ — Python is allowed HERE ONLY

Per the handout: the systems core is C; the interface layer may use anything, but **no
graded mechanism may hide in it.** Nothing in this directory is part of the shipped
product's runtime path.

**Present:**

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `board_sync.py` | Mirrors the checklist in `docs/milestones.md` onto GitHub issues and the project board. Not a product tool at all — it is how the plan is maintained. See `docs/BOARD/BOARD.md`. |

| --- | --- | --- |
| fast blink (~4 Hz) | **degraded** — a child is down, the adapter silent while the engine runs, storage failing, or undervoltage | highest |

## C. Storage and data integrity

### D.1 — Self-trained model; training in Python, inference in C 🔒

`D-004` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden (confirmed with instructor)
· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

A locally-trained, self-authored model is permitted; hosted APIs and third-party
pretrained weights are not. Therefore: training in `tools/train/`, weights versioned under
`models/` with the training commit in the header, **inference in C in `src/analysis/`**, no
network at runtime.

**Why inference in C.** First and most important for the grade: the runtime path sits
inside the supervised multi-process architecture, and a Python process there muddies the
boundary a grader must verify in sixty seconds. Second: it removes an interpreter, a
garbage collector and ~30 MB of RSS from a 48-hour memory-stability test we are graded on.

**What the model is not doing.** The features are the intelligence — operating-point
binning, per-bin baselines, Mahalanobis residuals, Theil–Sen trends, all hand-written.
Delete the weights file and the system still produces residuals and trends; it loses only
the final labeling step. That separation is deliberate and it is the answer at the defense.

### D.2 — Analysis pipeline shape 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

Operating-point binning (RPM × load × coolant temp) → per-bin running mean/variance →
multivariate residual (Mahalanobis) → robust trend (Theil–Sen) → classifier → state
machine with hysteresis and dwell.

**Why binning comes first.** Comparing a cold idle to a warm cruise is a false-alarm
generator. Every comparison happens inside one bin, against genuinely comparable
conditions. This single step removes more false positives than anything else downstream.

**Why multivariate.** The signal is the *correlation between sensors*, not any single
sensor's value — oil pressure is supposed to rise with RPM. A measure of anomaly that
already accounts for normal partnerships, and alarms only when a partnership breaks, is
what makes this something a threshold provably cannot do (handout §3.3).

### D.3 — Hysteresis and dwell before any verdict surfaces 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

No verdict reaches the user until it has persisted. Trip and un-trip levels differ
deliberately.

**Why.** A monitor that cries wolf twice gets unplugged, and an unplugged monitor is worse
than none because someone far away believes it is on duty. **False-positive rate is a
first-class metric in `docs/EVALUATION.md`, not an afterthought.**

### D.4 — The threshold test, as a standing rule 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

Every diagnostic we ship must require at least two cooperating sensors to reach its
conclusion. If a single threshold on a single value could produce the verdict, it is not
intelligence and it does not count. **Write the reason down in `docs/DESIGN.md` when
adding a diagnostic** — this is checked at the defense.

/* Single-producer / single-consumer lock-free ring from capture to storage. It is the
 * handoff mechanism E's process boundary needs, and mechanism F only if a Pi-side sensor
 * gives it a high-rate stream (D-017).
 *
 * The no-drop guarantee is the point. A gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis,
 * so a drop must be impossible to hide: every slot carries a sequence number and the
 * consumer accounts for every one of them. If the ring is full the producer must
 * report the overrun rather than silently overwrite an unread sample (DECISIONS B.3).
 *
 * Layout is fixed so the ring can live in shared memory across the process boundary
 * that mechanism E requires.
 */
#ifndef CARWATCH_RING_H
#define CARWATCH_RING_H

#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#define RING_CAPACITY 4096u   /* power of two — the mask depends on it */
#define RING_PAYLOAD    16u   /* bytes; a Mode 01 reply's data (<= 4 bytes) fits with room */

typedef struct {
    uint64_t seq;                    /* monotonic, never reused */
    uint64_t mono_ns;                /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC at capture */
    uint32_t pid;                    /* (mode << 16) | PID — room for 16-bit Mode 22 PIDs */
    uint8_t  len;
    uint8_t  src;                    /* data_src_t — live | replay | synth */
    uint8_t  _pad[2];
    uint8_t  data[RING_PAYLOAD];
} ring_slot_t;

typedef struct {
    _Atomic uint64_t head;           /* producer writes */
    _Atomic uint64_t tail;           /* consumer writes */
    _Atomic uint64_t overruns;       /* refused pushes — must stay zero */
    uint64_t         _pad[5];        /* keep head/tail off one cache line */
    ring_slot_t      slot[RING_CAPACITY];
} ring_t;

void     ring_init(ring_t *r);

/* Returns false when full. Never overwrites an unread slot; increments overruns. */
bool     ring_push(ring_t *r, const ring_slot_t *in);

/* Returns false when empty. */
bool     ring_pop(ring_t *r, ring_slot_t *out);

uint64_t ring_overruns(const ring_t *r);
size_t   ring_depth(const ring_t *r);

#endif

content.text:
Everything below is what the repo says today, with its status marked: ✅ built, 🟡 stub or planned, ⚠️ unreviewed decision. The last section lists what we agreed this session that the repo doesn't say yet, and a few places where the repo contradicts itself.

## 1. What it is

carwatch is an always-on in-vehicle diagnostic recorder for one car. It learns what that car normally does, flags behavior that leaves it before a check-engine light would, and names the likely fault area. The repo calls it a rough first draft: one car, one adapter, one Pi.

The claim we defend (D-021) is: *"learns this car's normal across its Mode 01 engine sensors, flags behavior outside it and names the likely fault area, with measured catch and false-alarm rates on faults we induce."* It does not claim to predict failure, work on any car, or track oil life.

The named user is Lance and his 2015 CR-V (PROBLEM.md). The reason it must be a device is that the signal only shows across all drives, including cold starts, and a phone app only captures trips someone remembered to record. Data also stays in the car with no account or upload.

## 2. Hardware and physical form

| Part | Role | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raspberry Pi 4 | The whole computer | — |
| OBDLink LX (STN chip, Bluetooth Classic SPP, not BLE) | Plugs into the OBD2 port; the Pi reads it over RFCOMM. Udev links it as `/dev/obd`; the daemon never opens an `rfcomm` number. | D-019 ⚠️ |
| Car USB-C port or 12 V-socket USB-C adapter (≥5.1 V/3 A) | Powers the Pi; nothing cut, spliced or pierced | D-011 ⚠️ |
| One LED + 330 Ω on GPIO17 (header pin 11, GND pin 9) | The warning light | D-014 ⚠️ |
| Food container | Enclosure (M4) | — |

Power is cut unannounced at every key-off. The Pi has no RTC. The adapter draws from OBD2 pin 16, which stays live with the key off, so its key-off current must be measured. The Pi's own radio is shared between the Bluetooth link and the phone Wi-Fi (`btcoex`). Stretch only: raw CAN via an MCP2515, taken up after D and E are measured.

## 3. How data enters: Mode 01

The capture daemon sends standard read-only Mode 01 requests (D-012 ⚠️). It sends them round-robin on a fixed rate-limited schedule, with one request outstanding at a time. At about 10 requests/s over about 8 PIDs, each PID gets about 1 Hz.

- Adapter init is `ATZ`, `ATE0`, `ATSP0` (auto-protocol).
- Every timeout and unanswered PID is logged. A PID the car stops answering is a fault signal, not a gap to fill.
- Link drops (read returns 0 or `EIO`, `POLLHUP`) are not crashes. The daemon reopens `/dev/obd` with backoff.
- Candidate PIDs: RPM `0x0C`, load `0x04`, coolant `0x05`, intake air `0x0F`, MAP `0x0B`, fuel trims `0x06`/`0x07`, O2, oil temp `0x5C`, fuel level `0x2F`, distance since cleared `0x31`. Oil pressure is expected to be absent. Mode 22 manufacturer PIDs are a stretch.
- The supported-PID survey decides the actual input list (`0100`, `0120`, `0140`, `0160` bitmaps).

## 4. The processes (mechanism E)

Four separate processes with separate address spaces, communicating over a shared-memory ring and Unix domain sockets (B.2 🔒):

| Process | Job | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `obdd` | Talks to the adapter, parses replies, pushes `ring_slot_t` into the ring with `src=live` | 🟡 stub |
| `storaged` | Drains the ring into the append-only log, recovers at boot | 🟡 stub |
| `analyzed` | Binning, baselines, residuals, trends, classifier, state machine | 🟡 stub |
| `supervisor` | Forks the children, `waitpid` loop, restart with exponential backoff and a restart-storm guard, hourly heartbeats, drives the LED, serves the UDS | 🟡 stub |
| `obdctl` | Query CLI over the UDS | 🟡 stub (usage text only) |
| status page | Read-only server for the phone, a supervised child | 🟡 not started |

Supervision rules (CLAUDE.md §2.6): clean exit codes, no orphaned fds across restart, a heartbeat within 60 s of start, and survives `kill -9` of any sibling. An unplugged sensor is not a crash, so it must degrade without a restart storm. The supervisor also runs under systemd `Restart=always`, so the device returns after each power cut.

**The ring (✅ built, tested).** 4096 slots, single-producer single-consumer, lock-free, laid out for shared memory. Each slot carries a sequence number, mono ns, PID (mode<<16 | PID), length, `src`, and 16 data bytes. When full, the producer refuses and increments an overrun counter; it never overwrites (B.3 🔒). The consumer accounts for every sequence number, so a gap means a detected loss.

## 5. Storage (mechanism D)

Records are append-only and never rewritten in place (C.1 🔒). Each is self-framing (magic `CWK1`) and CRC32'd over its whole body. The header has version, length, seq, mono ns, wall ns, `src`, `kind`, and crc32. Recovery scans from the last good offset, verifies CRCs, truncates the torn tail, and logs exactly what was lost.

- **Kinds:** raw adapter line (kept for replay), decoded sample, baseline (must survive power loss), verdict, fault event, heartbeat.
- **Provenance (C.2 🔒):** every record and log line carries `src=live|replay|synth`, never optional.
- **Open:** final on-disk layout (`recfmt`) and fsync batch size and interval (`fsync`). The repo requires the argument written in DESIGN §4 before the code.
- **Built:** CRC32 and its test. `storaged` itself is a stub.

## 6. The intelligence (all ours)

The pipeline (D.2 🔒): operating-point bin (RPM × load × coolant temp) → per-bin running mean/variance (Welford) → multivariate residual (Mahalanobis) → robust trend (Theil–Sen) → fault-area classifier → state machine with hysteresis and dwell.

- **Binning comes first** so every comparison is cold-vs-cold, warm-vs-warm. It removes more false alarms than anything downstream.
- **Hysteresis and dwell (D.3 🔒):** no verdict reaches the user until it persists, and trip and un-trip levels differ. False-positive rate is a first-class metric.
- **Threshold test (D.4 🔒):** every diagnostic needs two cooperating sensors, with the reason written in DESIGN.
- **Classifier (D.1 🔒):** trained by us in Python in `tools/train/`, weights in `models/` with the training commit in the header. Inference is C we wrote in `src/analysis/`. No third-party weights, no network. With the weights deleted, the system still produces residuals and trends and loses only the area label.
- **Fault areas (first draft):** cooling, air/fuel mixture (vacuum leak, MAF, O2), sensor or electrical, and "unusual, area unknown". Induced ground truth (E.2): disconnect a small vacuum line, partly block the radiator with cardboard, unplug a sensor.
- **Cut order if time slips:** the classifier first, then the phone page, then extra `obdctl` verbs.

## 7. Interfaces

**`obdctl`** has five verbs: `status` (liveness, per-process RSS, event counts), `verdicts [--since]`, `series PID --from --to`, `baseline PID`, `faults`. It is the primary interface and everything graded must be demonstrable through it.

**Phone page (D-013 ⚠️):** the Pi runs its own WPA2 Wi-Fi AP with no upstream. The page is read-only, shows only status and current verdicts, and has no state. The server language is an open sub-decision, with C recommended. It binds only to the AP interface and may live only in `src/interface/`.

**Warning light (D-014 ⚠️):** written only by the supervisor.

| Light | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Fast blink (~4 Hz) | Degraded: child down, adapter silent while engine runs, storage failing, undervoltage |
| Double-blink, pause | A verdict has surfaced |
| Slow blink (~1 Hz) | On duty, nothing to report |
| Steady on or off | Not running; never a valid state |

## 8. Logging, soak and fixtures

- **Logs** are structured and machine-parseable. `log_heartbeat` records liveness, RSS and event/drop counts hourly. `log_init` and `log_set_src` set the component and provenance. Built and in use.
- **Soak (handout §3.4):** timestamped startup, hourly heartbeats, at least one injected fault with detection, degradation and recovery visible, and an orderly end. Logs are raw and never tidied. `make soakcheck` runs a one-hour miniature, and `soak/run_soak.sh` and `inject_fault.sh` exist. The repo's open question (D-006) is the fake port versus live sensors.
- **Replay:** `tools/replay.py` feeds a labeled capture through the real pipeline. Output is labeled `replay`. `obdsim.py` (a fake ELM327 on a pty, labeled `synth`) is planned, not written.

## 9. Hard boundaries

No hosted models or network calls; the only network code is the status page's AP listener. No third-party weights. The device works with the network unplugged. C17 with `-Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wvla`, every allocation checked, every syscall error handled and logged. Python only in `tools/` and `ui/`. `make boundary` enforces the no-network rule. The mechanism comparisons (`expcrash` for D, `expkill` for E) are required experiments. Deliverables are DESIGN, EVALUATION, the README, soak logs, and transcripts.

## 10. Disagreements and gaps in the repo

These are real issues I found while reading, apart from what we agreed:

1. **Ring consumers.** DESIGN §1 draws the SPSC ring feeding `storaged`, `analyzed` and `obdctl`, but a single-consumer ring has one consumer. Either there are two rings or `analyzed` reads from `storaged`, and the diagram is vague on this.
2. **Status-page process.** It isn't in the Makefile's daemon list, and the source map doesn't say where its code lives.
3. **Stale references.** The D.2 rationale still uses oil pressure as its example. The schematic block list still includes a CAN block, though D-019 removed CAN. The `record.h` comment says "see D-00x" for the wall clock.
4. **Unfilled placeholders.** DESIGN has `[N]` rates, the failure-mode Response and Log columns, the storage figures, and the evaluation Targets all blank.
5. **Scripts.** `provision_pi.sh` and `install.sh` are TODO stubs that exit 1.

## 11. Agreed this session, not yet in the repo

- The Forester (2008, NA) is Camden's testbed alongside Lance's CR-V; nothing restricts either car.
- The 48 h soak means 48 h wall-clock of normal use, with auto-boot and key-off power cuts each drive. This still needs the professor's written confirmation.
- Crash-consistent only, no clean-shutdown hardware.
- Mechanism D gains WAL-style transactions and A/B checkpoints (extending C.1).
- No pre-assigned task owners; ownership by first commit.
- `pisensor` declined for now.

1. **Is the socket switched?** This now decides how the whole key-cycle story works, and it's the free test I mentioned: plug in any USB charger with an LED, turn the key off, and watch. content.text:
This is a better product. It also changes several earlier decisions, so here is the design on paper, still nothing written to the repo.

## The box

```text
 any USB-C source ─▶ [USB-C sink: 5 V only] ─▶ [charger + power-path] ─▶ [5 V 3 A boost] ─▶ Pi 4
 (their own charger)                              │      ▲
                                                  ▼      │ supplements weak input
                                              [rechargeable cell + protection + temp sensor]
 Pi GPIO ◀── "external power present" signal
 Pi GPIO / RUN pin ◀── wake button
 Pi GPIO ──▶ warning LED (D-014)          OBD2 BT dongle ~~ Bluetooth ~~ Pi
```

We buy the Bluetooth dongle and a USB-C cable; the user supplies the charger. We design the box around the Pi.

## How each wish maps to a mechanism

| You want | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| Safely limit power from any source | The input is a plain USB-C sink with 5.1 kΩ CC resistors, so a source only ever offers 5 V. The charger IC limits input current and has over-voltage protection for bad sources. |
| Supplement weak power | Power-path (load-sharing) charging: when the Pi draws more than the source offers, the cell covers the difference. This also covers the dip at crank. |
| Restrict too much power | Input current limit set below the source's rating, plus OVP. A source can only push what the sink draws. |
| Clean shutdown | A GPIO senses when external power disappears. The supervisor waits out a short grace period (so a crank dip isn't a shutdown), commits the WAL batch and checkpoint, `sync`s, then halts. A small cell is plenty, because a clean halt needs well under a minute of power. |
| Wake button before starting | A press brings the Pi up from halt, so it's ready at key-on. On a Pi 4 this is likely the RUN pin or the power stage's on switch; verify on the board before relying on it. |
| Auto-boot on next start | When the output is cut after halt, the power stage must re-enable when external power returns. This is a requirement on whichever part we choose. |

## What it changes in the decisions

- **D-024 reverses.** Clean shutdown is now the normal path. Crash consistency (D-025, WAL and checkpoints) stays as the guarantee for when the cell is dead, removed, or the plug is yanked. The design now has both layers, and the soak shows both.
- **D-011 is rewritten.** The box has a USB-C input and a cell. The lighter-socket adapter and the car-USB assumptions both go.
- **The measurements** become: input limit works, crank dip is covered, grace period never false-triggers, shutdown completes inside the cell's runtime, cold and hot cell behavior.
- **Hardware becomes real work.** The Power block of the KiCad schematic is now a power-path and cell circuit, not "a USB-C cable". The CAN block is obsolete (D-019). The Pi interface block gains the power-good signal, the button and the LED.

## Honest risks

1. **A lithium cell in a car is the biggest safety issue.** Cabins reach 60 °C or more parked in sun and drop below freezing in a Colorado winter. Standard Li-ion/LiPo must not charge above about 45 °C or below 0 °C, and many cheap UPS boards have no temperature cutoff. I recommend LiFePO4, or a charger with an NTC input that inhibits charging out of range, and a protected cell. I haven't verified specific parts, so these need datasheet checks. I'd treat this as a design requirement before any purchase.
2. **An always-on source breaks the key-cycle assumption.** If the user's USB port stays live with the key off, "external power lost" never fires. The box would need another way to know the car is off, for example the OBD data itself (RPM zero, or the control-module voltage PID if the car publishes it). The PID survey would tell us. This is more reason the survey is the first gate.
3. **Scope.** Building a power-path from modules adds wiring and failure modes. An off-the-shelf Pi UPS HAT is faster but gives us less to defend. A module-level design with a KiCad schematic gives us real hardware to defend at the cost of more risk.

## Questions

1. Build level: **module-level** (commodity charger, cell and boost modules, wired to a KiCad schematic we draw), or **an off-the-shelf UPS HAT** for the first build with the schematic documenting it? I recommend module-level, but only if you're willing to add power testing to M2.
2. Should the box assume a **switched** source (power drops at key-off) or work with **either** (detects key-off from OBD data when the source stays live)? I recommend "either", with switched as the common case.
3. Battery chemistry: are you okay with me specifying **LiFePO4 or a temperature-gated charger** as a hard requirement?

Written for: you, as the product definition to approve before any repo edits. Everything below is a proposal on paper, and the numbers marked "estimate" are mine, not measurements.

## The product in one sentence

A small, sleek plastic box with one USB-C port and one three-color light. It sits in the car, powers up when the car's power appears, records and analyzes what the Bluetooth OBD2 dongle reports, and shuts itself down cleanly when power goes away. A phone joins its Wi-Fi to see the data or download a report.

## What you'd see and touch

| Feature | Spec |
| --- | --- |
| Shell | Plastic, roughly 95 × 65 × 30 mm for a Pi 4 plus the power board (estimate). Vent slots, no metal around the radio. |
| Port | One USB-C input, and that is the only power connection. The user brings their own charger and cable. |
| Light | One tri-color LED (details below) |
| Buttons | None. See "Wake button" below. |
| Mounting | Velcro or a small bracket, glovebox or under a seat. No cabin wiring except the one USB-C cable. |

## The light

| Color | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Green | Booted, recording, all systems go. |
| Yellow | Transition on stored power only: starting up or shutting down. |
| Red | An issue: a child process is down, the OBD link is silent while the engine runs, storage is failing, or a surfaced verdict. |
| Off | Not running. This is the normal state when parked. |

One design question remains, and it's yours: in D-014, steady-on never counted as "alive" because a crashed controller can freeze a GPIO in its last state and show a false all-clear. With three colors I'd keep that safety by having green slow-pulse rather than hold steady. You decide whether that's acceptable. Also, is "issue" a problem with the box, a problem with the car (a verdict), or both?

## The power system: why a supercapacitor, not a battery

You said the stored power only needs to cover a clean shutdown (seconds) and bridge the crank dip, never run for minutes. That is exactly a supercapacitor's job, and it removes the biggest safety problem from my last message.

- **No lithium cell.** No thermal runaway, no charge-temperature cutoff to design, and no cell to degrade in a hot or frozen car. Supercaps tolerate roughly -40 °C to +65 °C or better, depending on the part.
- **Size estimate.** A Pi 4 draws about 3–4 W while shutting down (estimate). A shutdown of 10–15 s through a 5 V boost converter at about 85 % efficiency needs roughly 50–70 J. A bank on the order of 10 F at about 5 V holds around 100 J usable (estimate), so there is margin. The crank dip of 1–3 s needs only about 10 J.
- **Charging.** An empty supercap looks like a short circuit, so the charger must limit inrush current, or a modest USB source will trip. That limit is also what protects the source from the box.
- **Safe failure.** A supercap bank stores a lot of energy at low resistance, so it needs a fuse, cell balancing for the two series cells, and a way to discharge it when the box is opened.

## What's inside the box

```text
 USB-C receptacle ─▶ [CC resistors: 5 V sink only] ─▶ [TVS + fuse + reverse protection]
                                                              │
                                  ┌───────────────────────────┴──────────┐
                                  ▼                                      ▼
                       [inrush-limited charger]                  [input current limit]
                                  │                                      │
                       [supercap bank + balancing]                       │
                                  │                                      │
                                  └──────▶ [power-path: source first, cap makes up the rest]
                                                      │
                                                [5 V ≥3 A boost/buck] ─▶ Raspberry Pi 4 ── microSD
                                                                          │   │   │
                           "external power present" ──▶ GPIO (shutdown trigger)  Bluetooth ~~ OBD2 dongle
                                                                              │   Wi-Fi AP ~~ phone
                                                    tri-color LED (3 GPIOs, resistors) ◀──────┘
```

**The parts that matter:**

1. USB-C receptacle with CC resistors, so any source offers only 5 V.
2. Input protection: TVS diode, resettable fuse, reverse and over-voltage protection.
3. Input current limit and supercap charger, with inrush control.
4. Supercap bank: two series cells, with balancing and a fuse.
5. Power-path stage that prefers the source and uses the cap only to fill gaps.
6. 5 V ≥3 A converter that keeps the Pi up while the cap discharges.
7. A "source present" signal to a GPIO.
8. The Pi 4 and the microSD card, with its own Bluetooth and Wi-Fi.
9. The tri-color LED on three GPIOs with resistors.
10. Thermal design: a heatsink on the Pi, vent slots, ABS/ASA or another heat-resistant plastic.

## Behavior

1. **Source appears.** The supercap charges, the converter starts, the Pi boots (yellow), then reaches ready (green).
2. **Crank dip.** The cap bridges the gap for a second or two and nothing resets.
3. **Source disappears.** After a short grace period, the supervisor commits the last batch and checkpoint, syncs the disk and halts. The light is yellow during this.
4. **Power stays off.** The converter turns off when the Pi has halted, so the cap doesn't sit powering a halted Pi.
5. **If anything fails** (cap empty, source yanked mid-write, cable pulled): the crash-consistent log from D-025 still recovers at the next boot.

The grace period is a real tension. It must be longer than a crank dip and shorter than the cap's runtime. If a dip is misread as key-off, the box finishes a clean shutdown and reboots, which is safe but annoying. The Forester's actual crank profile settles this, so it needs measuring.

## Wake button

I'd drop it. A seconds-scale supercap can't boot a Pi that takes tens of seconds, so pressing a button before the key is on would have no energy to boot with. If the source is live (ACC), the box auto-boots anyway. You also asked for a clean port and one light, which is simpler without it.

**Boot time is also the honest weak spot.** A stock Pi 4 takes about 25–40 s to boot (estimate), not a few seconds. A trimmed image can get it lower, but I haven't measured it. It matters because the engine's cold-start warm-up is exactly what the analysis wants, so the first part of each drive may go unrecorded. That belongs in the design doc as a cost.

## Phone access

- The Pi runs its own Wi-Fi access point with no internet (D-013).
- A read-only page shows status, current verdicts and trends, and a download button produces a report file (HTML or CSV).
- A native app is possible later, but a web page works on any phone with nothing installed, so I'd defer the app.
- **Because the box is off when parked, it's viewable only while the car is on.** There's a nice side effect: plug it into any phone charger at home, and it boots and serves the same page.

## Hardware risks and things to measure before building

Per the repo's rule, these are measurements, not opinions:

1. Pi 4 current draw during boot, idle and shutdown, with a USB power meter.
2. Real boot time on a trimmed Raspberry Pi OS.
3. The Forester's crank dip: voltage on the source at the moment the starter turns.
4. Supercap discharge time into the Pi, to size the bank.
5. Pi temperature in the sealed box in a hot cabin.
6. Bluetooth and Wi-Fi sharing the one radio, with the plastic shell.

## What would change in the repo, one commit each

- D-011 rewritten to the USB-C input, supercap and light-only box.
- D-014 rewritten to the three-color light.
- D-024 revised: clean shutdown is the normal path, crash consistency is the fallback.
- D-013 extended to a report download, with an app only as a stretch.
- `wiring.md`, `BOM.md` and the schematic's Power and Pi-interface blocks.
- The README's hardware section, and DESIGN §1 and §5.
- A new failure-mode row set: cap empty, source yanked, grace-period misfire, thermal throttle.

## Questions

1. Is "red" a problem with the box, a problem with the car, or both?
2. Pulse or steady green? (Frozen-GPIO safety against a clean look.)
3. Okay to drop the wake button?
4. Should the plan stay with the Pi 4, or consider a Pi Zero 2 W for a smaller box? The repo notes it compiles slowly, and I haven't checked whether it handles the analysis load.

All ⚠️ UNREVIEWED, one commit each:

6. **D-011 rewritten** One USB-C input and a supercap bank, power off at rest.

3. **Boot-time budget.** What a stock boot costs, what a trimmed image could save, and what the first minute of each drive loses.
4. **Report spec.** What the downloadable report contains, so the analysis outputs have somewhere to land.
5. **Failure-mode rows** for the new hardware: bank empty, source yanked, grace misfire, thermal throttle, SD failure.
6. **Measurement plan** listing everything that needs a meter or a car before we trust a number, and which of those you can do for free first.

=================== docs/PROCESS.md # Process: why the rules are shaped this way `CLAUDE.md` holds the rules, short enough to load every session. This file holds the reasoning behind them, the worked examples, and the one-time setup. Section numbers in parentheses name the `CLAUDE.md` rule each part explains. **Read this when** a rule looks arbitrary, when you are about to argue for an exception, or before the defense. ## Why the git history is graded (§7) **This section is not advisory.** Our process grade is computed from transcripts corroborated against commits; the git history is itself a graded deliverable; and neither partner will break down a thousand-line diff to review it. A commit small enough to review in ninety seconds is a commit that actually gets reviewed. ## Commit granularity (§7.3) **There is no line-count limit.** A commit is sized by *what it is responsible for*, not by how big the diff happens to be. A 200-line rewrite of a single function is **one** commit; splitting it would force the reviewer to hold half a function in their head across two reviews, which is worse than the problem it solves. Twenty lines spread across five unrelated concerns is **five** commits, even though it is small. **The test that decides it, every time:** > Can the reviewer evaluate this as a **single yes-or-no decision**? If approving requires accepting one part while objecting to another, it is more than one commit. If rejecting any part means rejecting the whole thing anyway, it is one commit — leave it alone. **The one-sentence test, restated.** State the commit's responsibility in one sentence without using "and". If you can, it is one commit no matter how many lines it took. If you cannot, split along the "and". ### For code The unit is **one behavior, one function, or one design principle applied.** - Tests ship **in the same commit** as the behavior they test. Same responsibility. - A refactor is its own responsibility — never folded into a feature. - Formatting, renames, and file moves are **separate commits, labeled as such**, so the reviewer skims them at speed instead of hunting for logic buried in noise. - Two subsystems means two commits, always, regardless of size. - **Every commit builds and passes tests on its own.** This is the one hard rule in this section — it is what makes the history bisectable and each commit reviewable in isolation. **Size as a smell, not a limit.** Past roughly 400 changed lines, stop and re-apply the one-sentence test — large diffs *often* contain a smuggled second responsibility. If it survives the test, commit it as one unit and **say in the `WHY` why it is indivisible.** Then the reviewer knows the size was considered rather than accidental. ### For documentation, Markdown, and data files The unit is **one resolved question or one decision** — not one file, not one section. - Closing one open question that touches a line in six tables across three files is **one commit.** Splitting it is actively harmful: the reviewer can no longer see that the change was applied *consistently*, which is the only thing worth checking. - A doc commit's diff is often wide and shallow. That is expected and correct. - Never mix a **content** change with a **reflow/reformat** of the same file — the content change disappears into whitespace noise. Reformat separately, or not at all. - Never mix filling in a TODO with restructuring the section around it. - Never mix a decision's *record* with its *implementation* across files in a way that hides one inside the other — but **do** keep a decision and the code that enacts it together when they are genuinely one change. **The check:** `git show ` should answer exactly one question a human asked. If it answers two, split. If it answers half of one, you committed too early. ### For schematics (§7.12) Commit granularity for `electricalDrawing/` follows the documentation rule, not the code rule: the unit is **one functional block or one resolved electrical question**. Wiring the whole Power block is one commit even if it moves fifty symbols. Renumbering references across the sheet is a separate, labeled commit — never folded into a wiring change, for exactly the reason formatting is never folded into logic. ## A commit message, worked (§7.4) The format itself is `.gitmessage` (enable it with `git config commit.template .gitmessage`). A real example: ```text M3 ipc: refuse push on full ring instead of overwriting WHAT: ring_push now returns false and increments an overrun counter when head - tail == RING_CAPACITY, rather than wrapping over slot[tail]. WHY: DECISIONS.md B.3 — a silent overwrite is a gap in the record, and a gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis. REVIEW: The memory ordering on the tail load. I used acquire so the producer cannot see a stale tail and wrongly declare the ring full; I am least sure whether relaxed would be sufficient here. VERIFY: make && make test && make asan — all green, test_ring 3/3. ``` ## Pull requests (§7.5) - **A PR is sized by its claim, not its diff.** If the title needs "and", split it. If a reviewer would have to approve part and object to part, split it. A PR that implements one coherent thing is the right size even when that thing was large — but say so in the body, and lay out the commit-by-commit list so the reviewer has a path through it. - **Past ~10 commits or ~600 changed lines, re-apply the test rather than obey a number.** Most PRs that big contain two claims; the ones that genuinely do not are fine. - **Draft at the first commit**, not at the end — so the partner can watch it grow and object early instead of at the finish line. - The "What I am least sure about" paragraph must not be empty. If everything is certain, you have not thought hard enough about the diff. - If a PR needs a diagram, an annotated log excerpt, or a timing capture to be understandable — put it in the PR body. Making the reviewer reconstruct context is how reviews stop happening. ## The merge gate (§7.6) **If the reviewer does not understand a line, the pull request does not merge.** The remedy is never "trust it." The remedy is, in order of preference: 1. Claude explains it in a PR comment, in plain language, tied to the requirement. 2. The commit is split further, so each piece is obvious on its own. 3. The code is rewritten more simply, even at a cost in elegance or a few instructions. Its emptiness is a recorded position, not an oversight. ## Sheet structure Lance has blocked out functional areas on the root sheet. Keep that shape; it maps onto the architecture, which makes both documents easier to defend: | Block | Contains | | --- | --- | | **Power** | USB-C input from the car (switched, D-011) as an off-sheet connector, the Pi's 5 V rail, bulk and bypass caps. **No** OBD2 pin 16 and no buck converter. | | **Pi interface** | 40-pin header, the warning-light LED + 330 Ω on GPIO17 (D-014), grounds | | **CAN** *(stretch only, D-019)* | OBD2 pin 6 / pin 14 / pin 5 via the Y-splitter, TJA1050 transceiver, MCP2515, crystal + load caps, termination jumper **drawn open** (D-011), `INT` to GPIO, SPI0 (CE0/MISO/MOSI/SCLK) | | **Sensors** *(conditional, D-006)* | MPU-6050 on I2C with pull-ups; DS18B20 on 1-Wire with its 4.7 kΩ | The OBD2 adapter is not on the schematic: it plugs into the car and reaches the Pi over Bluetooth (D-019), so no wire of ours touches it. ## Rules 1. **Every net that leaves a block is a named label**, not a wire crossing a boundary. The netlist is read by humans at the defense. 2. **Annotate the voltage domain on every power net** (`+5V_USB`, `+5V`, `+3V3`). The Pi has no 5 V-tolerant inputs and no over-voltage protection; a mislabeled rail is how a Pi dies silently in Week 13. 3. **Every IC gets its decoupling drawn**, even when the module already has it. The schematic documents what is *electrically true*, not what we happened to buy assembled. 4. *(CAN stretch only.)* **The MCP2515 crystal frequency is a value field, not a comment** — 8 MHz vs 16 MHz changes the device-tree overlay, and a wrong value produces a silently dead bus. 5. **No `DNP`/`no-connect` without a reason in the field.** Floating inputs are an ERC violation for good reasons. 6. **`make hwcheck` green before the PR.** ERC violations are build failures, exactly like `-Werror`. ## What must not be trusted to a datasheet alone *Applies only if the CAN stretch goal is taken up.* The cheap MCP2515 breakout modules vary: some run the TJA1050 at 5 V and level-shift the controller side, and some do not — those drive **5 V onto MISO** and will kill a Pi. **Meter it. With the Pi disconnected. Before anything is plugged in.** This is the exact case `CLAUDE.md` §8.4 covers: no hardware conclusion from a verbal description or a datasheet, on a board nobody has measured. Record the measured voltages in `docs/hardware/wiring.md` with the date. ## Generated, never hand-edited `make hwdocs` regenerates these from the schematic. If a pin table and the schematic disagree, the schematic wins and the table was stale: - `docs/figures/electricalDrawing.svg` — rendered schematic, **committed**, so pull requests show a picture instead of an S-expression diff - `docs/hardware/bom.csv` — parts list feeding `BOM.md` - `electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.net` — netlist, the source for `wiring.md` pin tables =================== .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md ## What this changes ## Why **Decision IDs touched:** **Milestone:** M **Mechanism affected (B / D / E / F / none):** ## Review this hardest ## What I am least sure about ## Commit-by-commit 1. 2. ## Verification — paste real output, do not summarize
make ```text ```
make test ```text ```
make asan ```text ```
## Reviewer checklist - [ ] I can explain **every line** of this diff in my own words - [ ] I can answer, for any line: what wakes this? what happens on error? what is freed and when? why can't this drop or reorder a sample? - [ ] Each commit is one idea, and builds and tests on its own - [ ] No formatting, renames, or unrelated refactoring mixed into a logic commit - [ ] No test was weakened, skipped, or deleted - [ ] No network call, no hosted model, no third-party pretrained weights - [ ] Any data that is not live is labeled `replay` or `synth` everywhere it appears - [ ] Every allocation checked; every syscall error path handled **and logged** - [ ] New decisions are in `docs/DECISIONS.md`, and I have signed the ones I agree with - [ ] **If I do not understand something, I have asked instead of approving** =================== .gitmessage M : WHAT: One sentence. What changed, mechanically. WHY: 1-3 sentences. The reason, tied to a requirement, a decision ID, or a measurement. Never "to improve things." REVIEW: What the reviewer should check hardest, and what I am least sure about. VERIFY: The exact commands run and their result. # area: obd | ipc | store | analysis | supervisor | interface | # common | build | tests | tools | soak | docs | process # # One responsibility per commit, sized by what it is responsible for, not by # line count (CLAUDE.md 7.3). The one-sentence test: if the summary needs "and", # it is two commits. Past ~400 changed lines, say in WHY why it is indivisible. # Banned: wip, fix, fixes, updates, misc, cleanup, changes, more work, # address feedback. # # Enable with: git config commit.template .gitmessage =================== .markdownlint.jsonc // markdownlint rules for every .md in the repo (D-018, docs/DECISIONS.md §F.4). // Read by the VS Code markdownlint extension and by markdownlint-cli2. { "default": true, // The docs were written to a 90-column wrap. Tables, code and headings cannot // wrap, so they are exempt. "MD013": { "line_length": 90, "code_blocks": false, "tables": false, "headings": false }, // HTML we use on purpose: collapsible PR sections and the small print under // generated tables. "MD033": { "allowed_elements": ["details", "summary", "code", "sub", "br"] }, // One table style everywhere: `| a | b |` over `| --- | --- |`. "MD060": { "style": "compact" } } =================== .markdownlintignore # The course handout, transcribed from the instructor's PDF. Not ours to reformat. docs/handout/ =================== .gitignore build/ *.o *.d *.so *.elf soak/logs/ fixtures/raw/ models/*.bin __pycache__/ .venv/ *.pyc .idea/ # --- KiCad ------------------------------------------------------------- # Commit: .kicad_pro .kicad_sch .kicad_pcb .kicad_sym .kicad_mod # sym-lib-table fp-lib-table *.kicad_dru # Ignore: per-user state, editor history, autosave, and derived artifacts. *.kicad_prl *-backups/ _autosave-* *.bak *.kicad_sch-bak *.kicad_pcb-bak fp-info-cache .history/ # Derived outputs — regenerate with `make hwdocs`, never hand-edit. electricalDrawing/gerbers/ electricalDrawing/erc.json electricalDrawing/drc.json =================== .github/workflows/board.yml #### # CI for the project board (CLAUDE.md 7.11, docs/BOARD/BOARD.md). # # Two guarantees, one workflow: # manifest - docs/milestones.md, the board, is well-formed (offline, always fast) # drift - GitHub actually matches it, i.e. nobody forgot to run sync # # plus a third, soft for now: every PR traces back to an issue. #### name: board on: pull_request: push: branches: [main] permissions: contents: read issues: read jobs: manifest: name: milestones.md is well-formed runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.12" - run: python tools/test_board.py drift: name: GitHub matches milestones.md runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: python-version: "3.12" # --no-board keeps this inside GITHUB_TOKEN's reach: user-level Projects # need a PAT, issues do not. The board follows from the issues anyway. # --check exits 1 when anything would change. - name: board_sync --check env: GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} run: python tools/board_sync.py --check --no-board pr-closes-issue: name: PR traces back to an issue if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' runs-on: ubuntu-latest # SOFT LAUNCH. Failing red on your own PRs while you are still learning the # flow teaches you to bypass the check, which is the opposite of the point. # Delete this line once the habit is set - target 2026-09-26. continue-on-error: true steps: - name: body must contain "Closes #" env: BODY: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }} run: | if printf '%s' "$BODY" | grep -Eiq '(close[sd]?|fix(e[sd])?|resolve[sd]?)[[:space:]]+#[0-9]+'; then echo "ok - PR closes an issue" else echo "::error::PR body has no 'Closes #'. CLAUDE.md 7.11: every PR traces back to an issue; if there is no issue, add a line to docs/milestones.md and sync first." exit 1 fi

28	10. [Required Use of Claude Code](#10-required-use-of-claude-code)
29	11. [Personalized Verification: Demo Day](#11-personalized-verification-demo-day)
30	12. [Deliverables (M5)](#12-deliverables-m5)
31	13. [Grading](#13-grading)
32	14. [The Reach: Put It in Front of the User](#14-the-reach-put-it-in-front-of-the-user)
33	15. [Whereto, from Here?](#15-whereto-from-here)
34	16. [Suggested Schedule](#16-suggested-schedule)
35	17. [Hardware Notes](#17-hardware-notes)
36	18. [Late Submission](#18-late-submission)
37	19. [The Spirit of This Project](#19-the-spirit-of-this-project)
38	20. [Version History](#20-version-history)
39	- [Appendix A — Sensor Starter List](#appendix-a--sensor-starter-list)
40	- [Appendix B — Sample Team CLAUDE.md](#appendix-b--sample-team-claudemd)
41	- [Appendix C — Problem Memo Template](#appendix-c--problem-memo-template)
42	
43	---
44	
45	> **Nota Bene:** The term project is done in **teams of exactly two**. Its shape will feel
46	> familiar from the assignments: Claude Code is required, your process is graded from your
47	> transcripts, and the whole thing ends with a live demonstration and an individual defense
48	> in which each of you answers for the code with your name on it. What's different is the
49	> problem. Nobody hands you this one. You will choose a user, choose their problem, and
50	> build a working device that solves it, subject to the guardrails in Section 3. And one of
51	> those guardrails deserves top billing, because it inverts the assignments' arrangement:
52	> **Claude Code is required in your workflow and forbidden in your product.** Every line of
53	> intelligence that runs on the Pi, every decision, detection, and diagnosis, must be code
54	> you wrote and can defend. The agent helps you build the machine. It is not allowed to be
55	> the machine.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## 1. Overview
60	
61	Every assignment in this course hands you a problem and asks for a program. The term
62	project reverses the polarity. It hands you a program-shaped hole in the world and asks you
63	to find it. You will design and build a working device (a Raspberry Pi, at least two
64	sensors, and software of your own) that does something a specific person actually needs
65	done. Not a demo of a sensor. Not a tutorial, reassembled. A device that could sit on a
66	shelf in that person's life and earn its electricity.
67	
68	The question that will follow you through this project, from the first memo to the final
69	defense, is this: **who wants this, and why doesn't a phone app already solve it?** The
70	second half of that question is quietly load-bearing. A phone runs its apps when someone is
71	looking at it. Your device has to be awake at 3 a.m., unattended, on the day the
72	interesting thing finally happens. Always-on, physically embedded, resource-constrained,
73	unsupervised: that's exactly the territory where processes, schedulers, interrupts,
74	storage, and IPC stop being lecture topics and start being the difference between a product
75	and a demo. You don't need to bolt operating-systems content onto this project. Choose an
76	honest problem and the operating-systems content will come to you. Uninvited, and usually
77	at inconvenient hours. The guardrails in Section 3 exist only to make sure the problem you
78	choose is honest.
79	
80	The project is deliberately open. The five concepts in Section 4 are seeds for your
81	ideation, not a menu to order from; the strongest projects most years are ideas we didn't
82	think of. What is *not* open is the standard of evidence. Your system must survive 48 hours
83	unattended and prove it with logs. Your claims about latency, throughput, and reliability
84	must be measurements, not adjectives. And at the end, each of you, separately, must be able
85	to stand in front of your own code and explain why it is the way it is. What is *not
86	expected* is perfection, and Section 5 says so at length. The world your device ships into
87	is imperfect. Your budget is finite, your sensors are cheap, and the project is graded
88	accordingly: on what you did with what you had, and on the honesty of the accounting.
89	
90	> ### Grading methodology and the demo you can't rehearse
91	>
92	> The term project accounts for **10% of your course grade** and is graded out of 100
93	> points, split the same way the assignments are: most of the points answer a question the
94	> artifacts can settle, and the rest answer a question only you can.
95	>
96	> **70 points attach to the work and its evidence:** the problem memo (5), the design
97	> document (10), the checkpoint demonstration (10), the final system with its 48-hour soak
98	> test (30), and the quantitative evaluation report (15). These are graded from things we
99	> can run, read, and re-measure.
100	>
101	> **The remaining 30 points are individual, and no teammate can earn them for you.** 10
102	> points come from the analysis of your Claude Code transcripts, on the same five-level,
103	> repository-corroborated scale used in the assignments. 20 points come from the demo-day
104	> defense: questions about lines of your own subsystems, one question from across the
105	> ownership boundary, a defense of one episode from your `PROMPTLOG.md`, and a small live
106	> modification you make to your own code, alone, at the keyboard, while we watch. So two
107	> partners can submit one flawless repository and still leave demo day with very different
108	> grades. The defense was never grading the repository. It was grading each of you.
109	>
110	> Why the split? Same reason as the assignments, scaled up. A device that works is a nice
111	> thing to have. But a pair of engineers who can each explain, unprompted, why their
112	> sampler can't drop a reading and what their watchdog does when a sensor gets unplugged?
113	> That's a nice thing to *become*, and it's the thing this course is actually for.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 2. Learning Objectives
118	
119	- Translate a real user's real problem into a system design, and defend every component of
120	  that design by the problem's demands rather than by habit.
121	- Build an embedded sensing product on Linux that exercises at least two
122	  below-the-application-layer mechanisms: device drivers, interrupt handling, real-time
123	  scheduling, custom storage, or multi-process architectures with fault isolation.
124	- Write the product's intelligence yourself (statistics, signal processing, state machines,
125	  control) and know precisely why a threshold wouldn't have sufficed.
126	- Engineer for unattended operation: supervision, recovery, log discipline, resource
127	  stability over days rather than seconds, and graceful degradation when hardware
128	  misbehaves.
129	- Evaluate a system quantitatively: design the experiments, take the measurements, and
130	  present latency, utilization, and reliability numbers you can stand behind under
131	  questioning.
132	- Collaborate as a two-person team with explicit ownership, mutual code review, and a
133	  development process (Claude Code included) that leaves a verifiable trail.
134	
135	### Project parameters
136	
137	| Item | Detail |
138	|---|---|
139	| **Team** | Exactly two students; individual grade components as noted in Section 13 |
140	| **Platform** | Any Raspberry Pi with the 40-pin header (Pi 5, 4, 3B+, or Zero 2 W); see Section 17 |
141	| **Sensors** | At least two physically distinct sensors that genuinely cooperate (Section 3.1) |
142	| **Language** | Systems core in C (C17 or C23), `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` clean; the interface layer may use anything, but no graded mechanism may hide in it |
143	| **Expected effort** | Approximately 45–60 hours per student across the semester, milestoned in Section 6 |
144	| **Tooling** | Claude Code is **required** in your workflow (Section 10) and **forbidden** in your product (Section 3.3) |
145	
146	---
147	
148	## 3. The Guardrails: What "Non-Trivial" Means Here
149	
150	An open-ended project needs a floor, or the path of least resistance becomes a Python
151	script that polls a sensor and prints a number. Five guardrails define the floor.
152	Everything above them is yours.
153	
154	### 3.1 Two sensors that cooperate
155	
156	Your device must incorporate **at least two physically distinct sensors**, and they must
157	**cooperate**: fused into one decision, correlated against each other, or feeding a single
158	shared pipeline whose behavior depends on both. Two independent demos stapled together at
159	the README do not satisfy this requirement. That's one sensor short of the assignment,
160	twice. Cooperation is also where the systems content hides. Two sensors almost never want
161	the same sampling rate, the same interface, or the same latency budget, and reconciling
162	those differences inside one program is the first real design problem this project hands
163	you.
164	
165	### 3.2 Below the application layer: the mechanism menu
166	
167	Your system must include **at least two** of the following mechanisms, implemented by you,
168	identified explicitly in your design document, and measured in your evaluation. This is the
169	guardrail that keeps the project an operating-systems project rather than a wiring
170	exercise.
171	
172	| # | Mechanism | What "measured" means |
173	|---|---|---|
174	| **A** | A kernel module or character driver for one of your sensors, exposing it via `/dev` or sysfs | Correct concurrent access; behavior under load; a clean `dmesg` |
175	| **B** | Interrupt-driven input, with a head-to-head comparison against a polling design | Event latency distribution and CPU utilization, both ways |
176	| **C** | Real-time scheduling (`SCHED_FIFO`/`SCHED_RR`) for a latency-critical path | Jitter and deadline-miss rate vs. the default scheduler, under load |
177	| **D** | A custom storage layer: ring buffer, append-only log, or small FUSE filesystem, with an explicit crash-consistency story | Write batching and `fsync` discipline; recovery after a mid-write power cut |
178	| **E** | A multi-process architecture: sensors isolated in separate processes, a hub aggregating over IPC (shared memory, message queues, or Unix domain sockets), a supervisor that survives any child dying | Kill any child at any time; the system degrades, logs, recovers |
179	| **F** | A high-rate sampling pipeline with a no-drop guarantee: lock-free or single-producer/single-consumer ring between capture and consumption | Sustained rate with zero drops, proven by sequence accounting, under CPU contention |
180	
181	Choose the two (or more) that **your problem demands**, not the two that look easiest. The
182	design document (Section 8) requires you to justify each choice from the user's
183	requirements, and the defense will test that justification. Figure 1 shows where these
184	mechanisms live in a reference architecture.
185	
186	### Figure 1 — A reference architecture, not a required one
187	
188	```
189	  sampler daemon        storage layer (D)        analysis engine              interface
190	  SCHED_FIFO (C),  shm  ring / append log,  mmap  your statistics,      UDS    CLI / LAN
191	  no-drop ring (F) ring crash-consistent    / mq  DSP, state machines  ─────▶  dashboard
192	
193	────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── kernel/user boundary ──
194	
195	  kernel space:  I2C / GPIO subsystems · your character driver (A) · IRQ handling (B)
196	
197	                                                                       supervisor /
198	                                                                       watchdog (E)
199	                                                              ▲ restart on hang or crash
200	
201	        Sensor A              Sensor B                Actuator
202	       I2C, 10 Hz         GPIO, event-driven         (optional)
203	```
204	
205	*Letters mark where the Section 3.2 menu mechanisms live; pick at least two, driven by your
206	problem.*
207	
208	Sensors enter through the kernel; a sampler moves data into a storage layer without losing
209	any; an analysis engine you wrote turns data into decisions; an interface lets a human see
210	them; a supervisor keeps the whole thing alive at 3 a.m. Your product may collapse, split,
211	or rearrange these boxes freely. The graded requirement is only that **at least two menu
212	mechanisms exist somewhere in it, below the application layer, written by you.**
213	
214	### 3.3 The intelligence is yours
215	
216	The running product **may not call a hosted model of any kind** (no Claude, no other LLM,
217	no cloud inference API) and **may not embed a pretrained model** unless you petition for it
218	in your design document and receive approval. All analysis, detection, diagnosis, and
219	decision logic must be code you wrote: rolling statistics, spectral features, sensor-fusion
220	rules, state machines, control loops. Libraries for mathematical primitives (an FFT, a
221	linear solver) are fine, provided you can explain what the primitive computes and why your
222	pipeline needs it.
223	
224	Two rules of thumb bound the requirement, one from below and one from above:
225	
226	- **From below:** if a single threshold could do it, it isn't intelligence, and your product
227	  must do something with its two sensors that an `if`-statement could not.

> artifacts can settle, and the rest answer a question only you can.
>
> **70 points attach to the work and its evidence:** the problem memo (5), the design
> document (10), the checkpoint demonstration (10), the final system with its 48-hour soak
> test (30), and the quantitative evaluation report (15). These are graded from things we
> can run, read, and re-measure.
>
> **The remaining 30 points are individual, and no teammate can earn them for you.** 10
> points come from the analysis of your Claude Code transcripts, on the same five-level,
> repository-corroborated scale used in the assignments. 20 points come from the demo-day
> defense: questions about lines of your own subsystems, one question from across the
> ownership boundary, a defense of one episode from your `PROMPTLOG.md`, and a small live
> modification you make to your own code, alone, at the keyboard, while we watch. So two
> partners can submit one flawless repository and still leave demo day with very different
> grades. The defense was never grading the repository. It was grading each of you.
>
> Why the split? Same reason as the assignments, scaled up. A device that works is a nice
> thing to have. But a pair of engineers who can each explain, unprompted, why their
> sampler can't drop a reading and what their watchdog does when a sensor gets unplugged?
> That's a nice thing to *become*, and it's the thing this course is actually for.

---

## 2. Learning Objectives

- Translate a real user's real problem into a system design, and defend every component of
  that design by the problem's demands rather than by habit.
- Build an embedded sensing product on Linux that exercises at least two
  below-the-application-layer mechanisms: device drivers, interrupt handling, real-time
  scheduling, custom storage, or multi-process architectures with fault isolation.
- Write the product's intelligence yourself (statistics, signal processing, state machines,
  control) and know precisely why a threshold wouldn't have sufficed.
- Engineer for unattended operation: supervision, recovery, log discipline, resource
  stability over days rather than seconds, and graceful degradation when hardware
  misbehaves.
- Evaluate a system quantitatively: design the experiments, take the measurements, and
  present latency, utilization, and reliability numbers you can stand behind under
  questioning.
- Collaborate as a two-person team with explicit ownership, mutual code review, and a
  development process (Claude Code included) that leaves a verifiable trail.

### Project parameters

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Team** | Exactly two students; individual grade components as noted in Section 13 |
| **Platform** | Any Raspberry Pi with the 40-pin header (Pi 5, 4, 3B+, or Zero 2 W); see Section 17 |
| **Sensors** | At least two physically distinct sensors that genuinely cooperate (Section 3.1) |
| **Language** | Systems core in C (C17 or C23), `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` clean; the interface layer may use anything, but no graded mechanism may hide in it |
| **Expected effort** | Approximately 45–60 hours per student across the semester, milestoned in Section 6 |
| **Tooling** | Claude Code is **required** in your workflow (Section 10) and **forbidden** in your product (Section 3.3) |

---

## 3. The Guardrails: What "Non-Trivial" Means Here

An open-ended project needs a floor, or the path of least resistance becomes a Python
script that polls a sensor and prints a number. Five guardrails define the floor.
Everything above them is yours.

### 3.1 Two sensors that cooperate

Your device must incorporate **at least two physically distinct sensors**, and they must
**cooperate**: fused into one decision, correlated against each other, or feeding a single
shared pipeline whose behavior depends on both. Two independent demos stapled together at
the README do not satisfy this requirement. That's one sensor short of the assignment,
twice. Cooperation is also where the systems content hides. Two sensors almost never want
the same sampling rate, the same interface, or the same latency budget, and reconciling
those differences inside one program is the first real design problem this project hands
you.

### 3.2 Below the application layer: the mechanism menu

Your system must include **at least two** of the following mechanisms, implemented by you,
identified explicitly in your design document, and measured in your evaluation. This is the
guardrail that keeps the project an operating-systems project rather than a wiring
exercise.

| # | Mechanism | What "measured" means |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | A kernel module or character driver for one of your sensors, exposing it via `/dev` or sysfs | Correct concurrent access; behavior under load; a clean `dmesg` |
| **B** | Interrupt-driven input, with a head-to-head comparison against a polling design | Event latency distribution and CPU utilization, both ways |
| **C** | Real-time scheduling (`SCHED_FIFO`/`SCHED_RR`) for a latency-critical path | Jitter and deadline-miss rate vs. the default scheduler, under load |
| **D** | A custom storage layer: ring buffer, append-only log, or small FUSE filesystem, with an explicit crash-consistency story | Write batching and `fsync` discipline; recovery after a mid-write power cut |
| **E** | A multi-process architecture: sensors isolated in separate processes, a hub aggregating over IPC (shared memory, message queues, or Unix domain sockets), a supervisor that survives any child dying | Kill any child at any time; the system degrades, logs, recovers |
| **F** | A high-rate sampling pipeline with a no-drop guarantee: lock-free or single-producer/single-consumer ring between capture and consumption | Sustained rate with zero drops, proven by sequence accounting, under CPU contention |

Choose the two (or more) that **your problem demands**, not the two that look easiest. The
design document (Section 8) requires you to justify each choice from the user's
requirements, and the defense will test that justification. Figure 1 shows where these
mechanisms live in a reference architecture.

### Figure 1 — A reference architecture, not a required one

```
  sampler daemon        storage layer (D)        analysis engine              interface
  SCHED_FIFO (C),  shm  ring / append log,  mmap  your statistics,      UDS    CLI / LAN
  no-drop ring (F) ring crash-consistent    / mq  DSP, state machines  ─────▶  dashboard

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── kernel/user boundary ──

  kernel space:  I2C / GPIO subsystems · your character driver (A) · IRQ handling (B)

                                                                       supervisor /
                                                                       watchdog (E)
                                                              ▲ restart on hang or crash

        Sensor A              Sensor B                Actuator
       I2C, 10 Hz         GPIO, event-driven         (optional)
```

*Letters mark where the Section 3.2 menu mechanisms live; pick at least two, driven by your
problem.*

Sensors enter through the kernel; a sampler moves data into a storage layer without losing
any; an analysis engine you wrote turns data into decisions; an interface lets a human see
them; a supervisor keeps the whole thing alive at 3 a.m. Your product may collapse, split,
or rearrange these boxes freely. The graded requirement is only that **at least two menu
mechanisms exist somewhere in it, below the application layer, written by you.**

### 3.3 The intelligence is yours

The running product **may not call a hosted model of any kind** (no Claude, no other LLM,
no cloud inference API) and **may not embed a pretrained model** unless you petition for it
in your design document and receive approval. All analysis, detection, diagnosis, and
decision logic must be code you wrote: rolling statistics, spectral features, sensor-fusion
rules, state machines, control loops. Libraries for mathematical primitives (an FFT, a
linear solver) are fine, provided you can explain what the primitive computes and why your
pipeline needs it.

Two rules of thumb bound the requirement, one from below and one from above:

- **From below:** if a single threshold could do it, it isn't intelligence, and your product
  must do something with its two sensors that an `if`-statement could not.

336	product is built on is that what kills the batch is almost never the moment anyone is

339	it's "what is wrong?" The distance between those two questions, between a reading and a
340	diagnosis, is exactly the distance your intelligence has to cover. No threshold covers it.
341
