343	order of magnitude, flowing through a storage layer of your own design (**D**), often behind
344	a no-drop pipeline (**F**). The intelligence is rolling statistics, rate-of-change

346	oscillates with a period and amplitude you can measure. A failing seal shows up as indoor

351	with a measured true- and false-positive rate against failure episodes you provoked on

353	is not a workaround but a method.
354	
355	### 4.4 Seed 3: "Did something happen while I was gone?" (explainable security node)
356	
357	Everyone with a door has asked the question. The commercial answer is four hours of footage
358	nobody will ever watch. This product's differentiator is one word: **explainable**. It
359	answers with a timeline (*3:12 p.m., something person-sized, eleven seconds, moving away*)
360	that a human can read in five seconds and interrogate afterward. The user is anyone who
361	wants that answer without becoming a security-camera hobbyist and, not incidentally,
362	without pointing an internet-connected lens at their own life. Like Seed 1, the absence of a
363	camera is a feature you can defend out loud.
364	
365	**Engineering:** PIR motion plus ultrasonic ranging in an interrupt-driven pipeline. That's
366	mechanism **B**, with the polling comparison built into your evaluation, and usually **C**,
367	because ranging an object during a two-second event is a latency budget you have to actually
368	meet rather than merely admire. The intelligence is fusion (*motion says something, range
369	says how big and how far*), debouncing, event segmentation, and the design of the timeline
370	itself. A log schema from which a human can reconstruct the truth is a genuine engineering
371	artifact, and it's the thing your demo-day answer to "was that the cat?" will be read from.
372	Speaking of the cat: it is this seed's honest adversary, and a magnetic reed switch on the
373	door is the cheapest ground-truth generator you will ever wire. Every real entry gets a free

410	"mean CO₂ by hour, weekdays, last month" in less time than the argument takes.

414	facilities record with a three-day hole has lost the argument it exists to win. Everything
415	persists through a storage layer (**D**) whose retention, rollup, and `fsync` policies you

427	## 5. Building in an Imperfect World
428	
429	Somewhere between the memo and the checkpoint, every team hits the same wall. It's worth
430	telling you now that **the wall is scheduled.** The sensor your design really wants is a
431	$400 thermal imager and your budget is $60. The $4 accelerometer you bought instead has a
432	noise floor sitting exactly where the interesting signal lives. The CO₂ sensor needs three
433	minutes to warm up and drifts with the weather. And the data you need at the scale you want
434	(a year of failing compressors, a winter of greenhouse nights, 104 labeled door events) does
435	not exist, can't be bought, and won't be gathered in one semester by one device on one
436	shelf. None of this means you chose the wrong project! It means the project has become real.
437	Engineering has been called the art of the possible. The phrase is not a consolation; it's
438	the job description. **The constraints are not in the way of the work. They are the medium
439	the work is done in.**
440	
441	The unproductive response is to stare at what can't be done. The productive one is to ask,
442	repeatedly and in roughly this order, what can:
443	
444	- **Substitute.** Downgrade the sensor; keep the problem. A PIR and a door switch see more
445	  of a household's rhythm than you'd guess a thermal camera was needed for. A microphone's
446	  RMS level is a serviceable occupancy proxy. And two cheap sensors that corroborate each
447	  other routinely outperform one expensive one standing alone. Notice that "corroborate each
448	  other" is Section 3.1 arriving early, wearing a budget. Record in the design document what
449	  you wanted, what you used, and what the substitution costs in capability.
450	
451	- **Make your own ground truth.** You can't wait for the bearing to fail, so you provoke the
452	  conditions and label the recordings: the taped washer, the loosened bolt, the greenhouse
453	  vent propped open on purpose, a one-week paper logbook of real door events. **Ten labeled
454	  recordings you made are worth more than ten thousand unlabeled samples you found**,
455	  because you know what yours mean. And at the defense, you will be asked how you know.
456	
457	- **Replay.** Build a harness that feeds recorded sensor streams through your real pipeline
458	  at real or accelerated speed. Now a month of "operation" fits in an afternoon, rare events
459	  can be rehearsed on demand, and regressions are caught by re-running last week. The
460	  harness is not a workaround to be embarrassed about. It's a legitimate systems artifact
461	  (real products are tested exactly this way), and building one that faithfully preserves
462	  inter-sample timing is engineering in its own right. **One rule, absolute: replayed or
463	  synthesized data is labeled as such everywhere it appears. In logs. In the report. In the
464	  demo. The 48-hour soak and the live demonstration run on live sensors; everything else may
465	  run on honest replay.**
466	
467	- **Narrow the claim.** Shrink the sentence until it is true. *"Detects the three faults I
468	  can induce on this compressor, with these error rates"* is a claim that survives
469	  cross-examination; *"predicts failure"* is not. A narrow claim, met and measured,
470	  outscores a broad claim that's gestured at. On this rubric, and on every rubric that
471	  matters after this course.
472	
473	What this means for your grade deserves to be said without hedging: **the term project does
474	not expect a perfect project. It expects an honest one that works.** We grade your reasoning
475	about constraints, never the absence of constraints, because the absence of constraints is
476	not a condition that occurs in nature. The design document has a home for this reasoning
477	(Section 8), and the evaluation report's limitations section is where it pays off. The team
478	that writes *"we wanted X, we could afford Y, and here is precisely what Y cost us"* has
479	demonstrated the exact judgment this course exists to build, and will be graded like it. The
480	team that quietly papers over the gap has converted an ordinary constraint (the most
481	ordinary thing in engineering) into an integrity problem. And that is the worst trade
482	available anywhere in this course. We live in an imperfect world. Every system you will ever
483	ship will ship into it. So you may as well learn to do it well, and without apology, now.
484	
485	---
486

camera is a feature you can defend out loud.

**Engineering:** PIR motion plus ultrasonic ranging in an interrupt-driven pipeline. That's
mechanism **B**, with the polling comparison built into your evaluation, and usually **C**,
because ranging an object during a two-second event is a latency budget you have to actually
meet rather than merely admire. The intelligence is fusion (*motion says something, range
says how big and how far*), debouncing, event segmentation, and the design of the timeline
itself. A log schema from which a human can reconstruct the truth is a genuine engineering
artifact, and it's the thing your demo-day answer to "was that the cat?" will be read from.
Speaking of the cat: it is this seed's honest adversary, and a magnetic reed switch on the
door is the cheapest ground-truth generator you will ever wire. Every real entry gets a free
label. **Scoped-down version:** three event classes (person-sized, small, unknown)
classified honestly, with the confusion matrix to prove it, beats ten classes classified
wishfully.

### 4.5 Seed 4: "Is this machine about to break?" (small-shop predictive maintenance)

There is an entire industry (vibration analysis, condition monitoring) built on the fact
that machines announce their failures early, in frequencies, to anyone equipped to listen.
Its instruments cost more than your car. Its customers are factories. The user here is
everyone below that line: the shop with one compressor, the makerspace with one 3-D printer,
the laundromat, the house with a furnace fan. The moment the product exists for is the new
noise that started on a Tuesday when nobody was in the room. We tend to light up on
discovering that the hobby-scale version of a real industry fits inside one semester and
about $18 in parts. That discovery is worth having. And nothing says it has to expire with
the course.

**Engineering:** an accelerometer (the MPU-6050's hardware FIFO is your friend) and a
temperature sensor. Mechanism **F** is nearly mandatory, because a dropped sample corrupts
the spectrum; this is the seed where the systems work and the analysis work hold each other
honest most tightly. **C** is close behind, and **A** is there for the ambitious. The
intelligence is feature extraction (FFT band energies, RMS trends) compared against a
healthy baseline you recorded yourself. **Where it bites, instructively:** you can't wait a
semester for a real bearing to fail. So you induce faults. Tape a washer to a fan blade for
imbalance. Loosen a mounting bolt. Run the printer with a dry rod. Record labeled captures
of each. That's not cheating; it's how the real industry builds its test sets, and Section 5
makes it doctrine. The scoped-down version is also simply the honest one: *"detects the
three faults I can induce on this machine, with these error rates"* survives a defense.
*"Predicts failure"* does not.

### 4.6 Seed 5: "Ask the room" (facilities query hub)

The user is whoever answers for a room that other people complain about: the practice-space
manager, the lab steward, the roommate whose name is on the lease. The complaints arrive in
the past tense. *"It was freezing in here yesterday morning."* *"It gets stuffy every
afternoon."* And no live dashboard on earth answers a past-tense question. The product is a
**memory for a building**: several sensors, a history, and an interface that can answer
"mean CO₂ by hour, weekdays, last month" in less time than the argument takes.

**Engineering:** three or more sensors (air quality, sound level, temperature) as isolated
processes feeding a hub over IPC. That's mechanism **E**, with real supervision, since a
facilities record with a three-day hole has lost the argument it exists to win. Everything
persists through a storage layer (**D**) whose retention, rollup, and `fsync` policies you
must actually decide rather than inherit. The intelligence is the query engine: time-range
selection, aggregation, alignment of multi-rate series, and cross-sensor correlation
(afternoon CO₂ tracking the sound level is an occupancy story told by two sensors that never
met). **Where it bites:** interface ambition. Resist the pretty web app. A crisp CLI with
five query verbs and exact semantics is more defensible, and far more extensible at the
live-modification station on demo day, than a dashboard with none. This is the seed for
teams who suspect they might enjoy building databases, because it is one, in miniature,
standing on an IPC layer they also built.

---

## 5. Building in an Imperfect World

Somewhere between the memo and the checkpoint, every team hits the same wall. It's worth
telling you now that **the wall is scheduled.** The sensor your design really wants is a
$400 thermal imager and your budget is $60. The $4 accelerometer you bought instead has a
noise floor sitting exactly where the interesting signal lives. The CO₂ sensor needs three
minutes to warm up and drifts with the weather. And the data you need at the scale you want
(a year of failing compressors, a winter of greenhouse nights, 104 labeled door events) does
not exist, can't be bought, and won't be gathered in one semester by one device on one
shelf. None of this means you chose the wrong project! It means the project has become real.
Engineering has been called the art of the possible. The phrase is not a consolation; it's
the job description. **The constraints are not in the way of the work. They are the medium
the work is done in.**

The unproductive response is to stare at what can't be done. The productive one is to ask,
repeatedly and in roughly this order, what can:

- **Substitute.** Downgrade the sensor; keep the problem. A PIR and a door switch see more
  of a household's rhythm than you'd guess a thermal camera was needed for. A microphone's
  RMS level is a serviceable occupancy proxy. And two cheap sensors that corroborate each
  other routinely outperform one expensive one standing alone. Notice that "corroborate each
  other" is Section 3.1 arriving early, wearing a budget. Record in the design document what
  you wanted, what you used, and what the substitution costs in capability.

- **Make your own ground truth.** You can't wait for the bearing to fail, so you provoke the
  conditions and label the recordings: the taped washer, the loosened bolt, the greenhouse
  vent propped open on purpose, a one-week paper logbook of real door events. **Ten labeled
  recordings you made are worth more than ten thousand unlabeled samples you found**,
  because you know what yours mean. And at the defense, you will be asked how you know.

- **Replay.** Build a harness that feeds recorded sensor streams through your real pipeline
  at real or accelerated speed. Now a month of "operation" fits in an afternoon, rare events
  can be rehearsed on demand, and regressions are caught by re-running last week. The
  harness is not a workaround to be embarrassed about. It's a legitimate systems artifact
  (real products are tested exactly this way), and building one that faithfully preserves
  inter-sample timing is engineering in its own right. **One rule, absolute: replayed or
  synthesized data is labeled as such everywhere it appears. In logs. In the report. In the
  demo. The 48-hour soak and the live demonstration run on live sensors; everything else may
  run on honest replay.**

- **Narrow the claim.** Shrink the sentence until it is true. *"Detects the three faults I
  can induce on this compressor, with these error rates"* is a claim that survives
  cross-examination; *"predicts failure"* is not. A narrow claim, met and measured,
  outscores a broad claim that's gestured at. On this rubric, and on every rubric that
  matters after this course.

What this means for your grade deserves to be said without hedging: **the term project does
not expect a perfect project. It expects an honest one that works.** We grade your reasoning
about constraints, never the absence of constraints, because the absence of constraints is
not a condition that occurs in nature. The design document has a home for this reasoning
(Section 8), and the evaluation report's limitations section is where it pays off. The team
that writes *"we wanted X, we could afford Y, and here is precisely what Y cost us"* has
demonstrated the exact judgment this course exists to build, and will be graded like it. The
team that quietly papers over the gap has converted an ordinary constraint (the most
ordinary thing in engineering) into an integrity problem. And that is the worst trade
available anywhere in this course. We live in an imperfect world. Every system you will ever
ship will ship into it. So you may as well learn to do it well, and without apology, now.

759	someone who does not care how it works is a different kind of artifact from software that
760	has only ever been demonstrated, and building the first kind, even once, changes how you

768	
769	Some of you will finish this project, look at the device sitting in its food-container
770	enclosure and think: *hang on, would somebody pay for this?* Hold onto that thought. It may
771	be worth more than the grade.
772	
773	Startups are rarely founded on a dazzling idea. They are founded on a problem somebody
774	already has and is already solving badly; usually with a spreadsheet and a bad habit.
775	Finding one of those is the hard part, and you were made to do it in Week 5, in front of a
776	skeptical reader. Your problem memo is structurally the opening of a pitch: who the user is,
777	what the problem costs them, why the obvious answer fails, and what you propose instead. The
778	same questions get asked later in nicer rooms with worse coffee.
779	
780	The next thing you have is rarer than you'd guess. An enormous quantity of software talent
781	can wrap a web API and call it a company. Much less of it can make a physical thing stay
782	alive, unattended, in a stranger's basement, through a power blip and a sensor that quietly
783	fell off in March. That is a real barrier to entry, and you now have 48 hours of logs saying
784	you cleared it.

786	You also have evidence. When a customer or an investor asks the only question that matters
787	("does it work?"), most people answer with adjectives. You can answer with a measured
788	false-positive rate and a limitations section you wrote when nobody was forcing you to be
789	honest. That habit will outlive every technology named in this handout.

793	a support inbox somebody has to read on a Sunday. No device survives contact with 50
794	strangers unchanged. Assume version two exists before version one leaves the bench.

846	## 19. The Spirit of This Project
847	
848	You are required to submit your own work, and you are required to use Claude Code to help
849	you produce it, and, new this time, you are required to keep the model out of the product
850	itself. These three requirements are one requirement wearing three hats: **the work must be
851	yours, where *yours* has never meant *unaided* and has always meant *understood, defended,
852	and extendable by you*.**
853	
854	There is no version of this project worth having that you didn't build. A repository
855	assembled by wholesale generation will be a stranger to you at the defense, where thirty
856	minutes with your own code costs more than the generation saved. A product that quietly
857	phones a model has outsourced exactly the part of the semester you were supposed to keep.
858	And a soak log that was tidied after the fact is the one artifact in this course we are best
859	equipped to notice, because real systems are never that tidy.
860	
861	But hold this next paragraph together with the previous one, because they are not in
862	tension: understand what is *not* being demanded of you. The device you ship in Week 15 will
863	be smaller than the one you imagined in Week 5. A sensor will have been substituted, a
864	feature cut, a claim narrowed. The enclosure will be a food container. One graph in your
865	evaluation will end in a shrug. **Good.** That shrinkage, honestly accounted for, is not the
866	project failing. It's the project working, because it's the exact shape of every real system
867	you will ever ship. Perfection is not on the rubric and never was. What is on the rubric is
868	a device that runs, numbers that are real, limitations that are named, and two people who
869	can each explain the distance between what they wanted to build and what they built. The
870	teams that struggle here are almost never the ones facing the most constraints. They are the
871	ones who spend the semester mourning the project they couldn't do instead of building the
872	one they could. Don't join them. When the ideal sensor turns out not to exist at your
873	budget, or the data you need refuses to exist at your scale, the assignment at that moment
874	is not to document an obstacle. It is to turn to what is actually on the bench and ask what
875	can be done with it. Which is, not incidentally, the question the entire history of good
876	engineering consists of asking.
877	
878	It's also worth saying plainly what this project is a rehearsal for, because it is not
879	really the Raspberry Pi. Every project you ship for the rest of your career will have a
880	stakeholder who cares about outcomes and not mechanisms, a budget that forecloses the
881	elegant option, a teammate whose code you must both trust and verify, a tool that is
882	confidently wrong at the worst possible moments, a deadline that does not move, and a world
883	that declines to be ideal about any of it. This project is that, at one-tenth scale, with
884	gentler consequences and better office hours. Learning to do good work inside those
885	conditions, not despite them, and never while waiting for them to lift, is the transferable
886	skill. **The drivers and ring buffers are the vehicle. The judgment is the cargo.**
887	
888	So do it the way it is designed to be done. Find a person with a problem. Build them a
889	machine that is awake when they are not. Use the agent as the collaborator it is (plan
890	first, keep the diffs small, demand evidence, merge nothing you can't explain) and write the
891	thinking parts yourself. Accept the constraints as the terms of the craft, and let the
892	limitations section tell the truth without flinching. At the end you'll have a device on a
893	shelf, doing a job, imperfectly and honestly, for someone who is glad it exists. Most
894	courses can't offer you that. This one is trying to.

906	## Appendix A — Sensor Starter List
907	
908	> **Quick flag:** anything marked **(!)** has 5 V lurking in it somewhere, so treat those
909	> interfaces with a little extra respect.
910	
911	Here's the thing about the Pi's GPIO pins: **they only speak 3.3 V logic, and there's zero
912	over-voltage protection built in.** Feed one a 5 V signal directly and it can just… die.
913	Silently. No warning light, no smoke, sometimes not even a clue until you notice nothing's
914	responding anymore. And sometimes it doesn't stop at the pin, it takes the whole SoC down
915	with it. That's exactly why the HC-SR04 needs a voltage divider on its echo line. The
916	trigger pin is fine with 5 V, but the echo pin is not, and if you wire them the same way
917	because "eh, they're both just signal pins," congratulations, you've found the single most
918	popular way to lose a Pi in Week 13.
919	
920	But **power-rail mistakes are even less forgiving.** Swap VCC and GND, or let a 5 V rail
921	touch the 3.3 V rail while you're poking around with a multimeter, and your board usually

The nine-step workflow from Assignment 0, Section 10 applies to this project verbatim:
persistent context in `CLAUDE.md`, explore before writing, plan mode first, tests leading,
evidence over assertion, context hygiene, adversarial review, git discipline, and
automation. Your transcripts will be read against it. This section covers only what changes
when the codebase is shared, the target is hardware, and the model is banned from the
payroll.

### 10.1 What changes in a team of two

- **One `CLAUDE.md`, two authors.** The file is team law: build and deploy commands, the
  hard constraints (no runtime model calls; no network dependence; every daemon
  supervisable), style rules, and the ownership map. Both partners maintain it. The agent
  reads it in every session, so a constraint that lives only in one partner's head protects
  nothing. A sample is in [Appendix B](#appendix-b--sample-team-claudemd).
- **Sessions are personal.** Each partner works in their own clone and their own Claude Code
  sessions, and submits their own transcripts. Your 10 process points are computed from
  *your* `.jsonl` files, corroborated against *your* commits.
- **Your partner is a reviewer the agent can't replace.** Every milestone's diffs get two
  reviews: a fresh-context agent review (Assignment 0, Step 7) and a human one by the
  partner who did not write the code. Each partner's `PROMPTLOG.md` must include at least
  one episode of reviewing the other's work: what you questioned, what the answer was, what
  changed. *A team whose two halves never disagreed about anything all semester has not been
  reviewing.*
- **Commits carry names.** At least **40 meaningful commits** across the project, with both
  partners well represented. A history in which one partner authored under a quarter of the
  substantive commits will be probed hard at the individual defense. Which, remember, is 20
  individual points.

### 10.2 What changes when the target is hardware

The agent can't see your breadboard and this cuts both ways. It will confidently reason
about a sensor it has never met, and it will be wrong in ways that only an instrument can
catch. So the evidence discipline of Assignment 0, Step 5 gets a hardware clause: **close
the loop with measurements.** Paste `dmesg` verbatim. Paste the timing capture. Paste
`/proc/interrupts` before and after. The agent reads a kernel oops better than a vague
description of one. And so will you, by the end of this project.

> Our DHT22 reads fail checksum roughly 30% of the time, but only when the analysis process
> is busy. Here is the pulse-width capture from the logic analyzer for one failed read:
> `[paste]`. Our read path bit-bangs from userspace via libgpiod. Identify where the timing
> budget breaks under scheduling delay, and propose two designs that survive it, with
> tradeoffs, before writing any code.

### 10.3 What changes because the model is banned from the product

Nothing about how you develop; everything about what you ship. Use the agent freely to plan
the supervisor, explain `epoll`, draft the FFT feature extractor, and generate labeled test
fixtures for your detector. But the shipped tree must honor Section 3.3, and **the boundary
must be legible: a grader reading your repository should be able to confirm in one minute
that the product's only network activity is its own LAN interface.** And if you're ever
tempted to resolve a hard analysis problem by "just asking a model" at runtime, notice that
the temptation *is* the assignment. The hard analysis problem is the part you are here to
learn to solve.

### 10.4 Prompt patterns: good vs. useless

| Useless | Effective |
|---|---|
| "make the sensor work" | "`i2cdetect` sees the BME280 at 0x76 but our reads return 0x80 in every field. Here is our init sequence and the datasheet's required mode transition [paste both]. Diff them and identify the missing step; do not rewrite the module." |
| "fix the crash" | "`dmesg` oops attached [paste]. The fault is in our driver's read path, which takes lock at line 84. Walk the call path from IRQ context and identify what we are doing there that IRQ context forbids." |
| "make it faster" | "`perf report`: 38% of sampler CPU in `memcpy`. Plan a zero-copy handoff from the capture ring to the consumer given single-producer/single-consumer and a 16 KiB budget. Risks and invariants first; no code." |
| "write the daemon" | "Plan the supervisor: restart policy with backoff, fd hygiene across fork/exec, and how we avoid a restart storm when a sensor is physically unplugged rather than crashed. List what you'd log at each decision." |
| "why is the soak failing" | "RSS grew 40 MB over 12 hours; hourly heartbeats attached. Rank hypotheses by likelihood given that event counts are flat but query counts are not, then propose the cheapest instrumentation to discriminate between the top two." |

**Transcript submission.** Identical to Assignment 0, per partner: the raw `.jsonl` session
files from `~/.claude/projects/`, copied in as-is. Not summarized. Not exported. Not
retyped. Work in a dedicated project directory per partner so the copy is one `cp`.
Transcripts are purged locally after 30 days by default, and this project spans more than 30
days, so copy them out at every milestone or raise `cleanupPeriodDays` now. **Losing Week-5
transcripts to the default in Week-15 is a foreseeable loss; foreseeable losses are not
excused.**

---

## 11. Personalized Verification: Demo Day

Every team demos live; every student defends individually. The session runs roughly thirty
minutes per team, in 3 movements.

**The demonstration.** Your device, running your soaked build, doing its job. At a moment of
our choosing, **we will inject a fault, most often by unplugging one of your sensors
mid-demo.** This is announced now so that nobody can call it unfair later. The graded
behaviors are graceful degradation, honest reporting through your own interface, and the log
line proving the system noticed. A device that freezes, lies, or crashes when hardware
misbehaves has failed its user at exactly the moment it existed for.

**The individual defense.** Separately, each partner answers for their own subsystems: lines
of your code (*"what wakes this thread?"*, *"what happens to this fd when the child dies?"*,
*"why can't this ring overwrite an unread sample?"*), one judgment call from your
`PROMPTLOG.md`, and one question from across the ownership boundary. Because owning your
half deeply does not excuse understanding the other half not at all.

**The live modification.** Each partner, alone at the keyboard, makes one small
previously-unseen change to their own subsystem, starting from the submitted source: a new
field in the heartbeat, a changed threshold semantic, a new flag on the query CLI. Small for
an author. Revealing for anyone else.

**Why this exists.** For the same reason it exists in the assignments, with the stakes
raised. A repository, a report, and a beautiful demo video can all be produced without
understanding. Thirty minutes of your own code behaving unexpectedly in front of you cannot.
The defense is not an audit bolted onto the project; it's the project's final measurement,
and the quantity it measures is *you*.

---

## 12. Deliverables (M5)

Submit, via Canvas, a tar file containing:

- **Source and build:** the full repository, with a `Makefile` (or equivalent) and a
  `README.md` that takes a TA from a clean Pi to your running system without your help. *If
  the TA can't boot it, the TA can't grade it.*
- **Documents:** `PROBLEM.md` (the memo, as revised), `DESIGN.md` (as it ended, not as it
  began, with a short changelog of what M2's version got wrong), and `EVALUATION.md`.
- **Soak evidence:** the raw, unedited logs of the 48-hour run, including the injected fault.
- **`CLAUDE.md`**, checked in and evolving across the milestones.
- **Per partner:** `PROMPTLOG.md` (6–10 annotated episodes, including one revised plan, one
  rejected diff, one tool-output debugging loop with real hardware evidence, and one review
  of your partner's work), `REFLECTION.md` (one page: where the agent was most and least
  reliable against real hardware; one bug it introduced that you caught, and how), and the
  raw `.jsonl` transcripts.
- **Git history:** ≥ 40 meaningful commits spanning the milestones, both partners
  represented. **A pair of "final submission" commits is an automatic process-grade of zero.
  For both partners.**

---

## 13. Grading

| Component | Method | Points | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Problem memo (M1) | Passes the phone-app test; user and problem concrete; risk named | 5 | team |
| Design document (M2) | Mechanisms justified from requirements; failure-mode table; evaluation plan; ownership map | 10 | team |
| Checkpoint demo (M3) | Both sensors through the real pipeline into real storage; one menu mechanism live | 10 | team |
| Final system (M4/M5) | All five guardrails met; runs from the README; survives our fault injection; 48-hour soak evidenced | 30 | team |
| Evaluation report (M5) | Quantitative, reproducible, includes the required mechanism comparisons, honest about limits | 15 | team |
| Process | Your transcripts on the five-level repository-corroborated scale of Assignment 0 (level 5 = 10 pts, each level down −2), read alongside your `PROMPTLOG.md` and commits | 10 | **individual** |
| Demo-day defense | Subsystem fluency, cross-boundary question, `PROMPTLOG` defense, live modification | 20 | **individual** |
| **Total** | | **100** | |
| The Reach | Deployment with the real user (Section 14): attempted for the craft, not for points | 0 | optional |

**Two clarifications.** First, the memory-bug discipline of the assignments carries over:
the systems core must be clean under `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, and **ASan/valgrind findings
in components where they apply cap that component's contribution to the final-system score
at 50%**, exactly as in Assignment 0. *A device that leaks for 48 hours and happens not to
die has not passed the soak. It has outrun it.* Second, the transcript scale is applied per
partner, to that partner's own sessions. Working in one shared login defeats this and will
cost both partners.

---

## 14. The Reach: Put It in Front of the User

This carries no points. Do it anyway. Install the device where the problem actually lives
(the parent's kitchen, the shop floor, the greenhouse) for at least a week, and add one page
to your reflection about what the user did with it, what surprised you, and what you'd
change now that a stranger has depended on your code. Nobody is checking whether you do
this. Which is exactly what makes doing it mean something. Software that has been used by
someone who does not care how it works is a different kind of artifact from software that
has only ever been demonstrated, and building the first kind, even once, changes how you
build everything after. And if you finish the week wondering whether the thing on that shelf
could become something more than a course project? That is not an accident, and my office
hours are open.

---

## 15. Whereto, from Here?

Some of you will finish this project, look at the device sitting in its food-container
enclosure and think: *hang on, would somebody pay for this?* Hold onto that thought. It may
be worth more than the grade.

Startups are rarely founded on a dazzling idea. They are founded on a problem somebody
already has and is already solving badly; usually with a spreadsheet and a bad habit.
Finding one of those is the hard part, and you were made to do it in Week 5, in front of a
skeptical reader. Your problem memo is structurally the opening of a pitch: who the user is,
what the problem costs them, why the obvious answer fails, and what you propose instead. The
same questions get asked later in nicer rooms with worse coffee.

The next thing you have is rarer than you'd guess. An enormous quantity of software talent
can wrap a web API and call it a company. Much less of it can make a physical thing stay
alive, unattended, in a stranger's basement, through a power blip and a sensor that quietly
fell off in March. That is a real barrier to entry, and you now have 48 hours of logs saying
you cleared it.

You also have evidence. When a customer or an investor asks the only question that matters
("does it work?"), most people answer with adjectives. You can answer with a measured
false-positive rate and a limitations section you wrote when nobody was forcing you to be
honest. That habit will outlive every technology named in this handout.

Now the part I owe you. The distance from a working prototype to a shippable product is
long: sourcing, enclosures, certification if you emit anything interesting, unit economics,
a support inbox somebody has to read on a Sunday. No device survives contact with 50
strangers unchanged. Assume version two exists before version one leaves the bench.

But if you are ever going to try this, the cheapest moment of your life is now! You have no
payroll and no mortgage. Plus there's a campus stuffed with resources you are already paying
for: the institute for entrepreneurship, pitch competitions, prototyping space, an IP
office, faculty who will read your business plan for the price of asking nicely. You also
have a co-founder (in your teammate) whose code you have already reviewed for fifteen weeks,
which is more due diligence than most founding teams ever manage on each other.

And if the answer turns out to be no? That is a perfectly good answer. You will still have
built a real thing for a real person, which was the point the entire time. My door is open
either way. Bring the food container.

---

## 16. Suggested Schedule

- **Weeks 3–4:** Form the team. Ideate widely (Section 4.1), then apply the guardrails as
  filters and Section 5 as the reality check. **Order hardware immediately. Shipping time is
  the most common silent schedule-killer.** → M0
- **Week 5:** Problem memo (M1). Get both sensors electrically alive on a breadboard while
  the memo is under review.
- **Weeks 6–7:** Design document (M2). Argue about the architecture now, in ink, while
  changing it is free.
- **Weeks 8–10:** Build the pipeline: capture, storage, supervision. Checkpoint demo (M3).
  **And start soak-style overnight runs now, at small scale; every leak found in Week 9 is a
  crisis avoided in Week 14.**
- **Weeks 11–13:** The analysis engine, the interface, the mechanism-comparison experiments,
  and the evaluation measurements.
- **Week 14:** Feature freeze (M4). Begin the graded 48-hour soak **with margin to run it
  twice. You will want to run it twice.**
- **Weeks 15–16:** Final submission (M5), demo day (M6), and, if you are wise, The Reach.

---

## 17. Hardware Notes

- **Boards.** Any Raspberry Pi with the 40-pin header works. A Pi 4 or 5 is the comfortable
  choice; a Zero 2 W is fine for the deployed device but slow to compile on, so develop on
  something larger or cross-compile.
- **GPIO is 3.3 V and unforgiving.** The Pi has no 5 V-tolerant inputs and no analog inputs
  at all. The HC-SR04's echo pin needs a voltage divider; analog sensors need an ADC (an
  MCP3008 over SPI is the standard answer).

---

## 18. Late Submission

See the course late-submission policy.

---

## 19. The Spirit of This Project

You are required to submit your own work, and you are required to use Claude Code to help
you produce it, and, new this time, you are required to keep the model out of the product
itself. These three requirements are one requirement wearing three hats: **the work must be
yours, where *yours* has never meant *unaided* and has always meant *understood, defended,
and extendable by you*.**

There is no version of this project worth having that you didn't build. A repository
assembled by wholesale generation will be a stranger to you at the defense, where thirty
minutes with your own code costs more than the generation saved. A product that quietly
phones a model has outsourced exactly the part of the semester you were supposed to keep.
And a soak log that was tidied after the fact is the one artifact in this course we are best
equipped to notice, because real systems are never that tidy.

But hold this next paragraph together with the previous one, because they are not in
tension: understand what is *not* being demanded of you. The device you ship in Week 15 will
be smaller than the one you imagined in Week 5. A sensor will have been substituted, a
feature cut, a claim narrowed. The enclosure will be a food container. One graph in your
evaluation will end in a shrug. **Good.** That shrinkage, honestly accounted for, is not the
project failing. It's the project working, because it's the exact shape of every real system
you will ever ship. Perfection is not on the rubric and never was. What is on the rubric is
a device that runs, numbers that are real, limitations that are named, and two people who
can each explain the distance between what they wanted to build and what they built. The
teams that struggle here are almost never the ones facing the most constraints. They are the
ones who spend the semester mourning the project they couldn't do instead of building the
one they could. Don't join them. When the ideal sensor turns out not to exist at your
budget, or the data you need refuses to exist at your scale, the assignment at that moment
is not to document an obstacle. It is to turn to what is actually on the bench and ask what
can be done with it. Which is, not incidentally, the question the entire history of good
engineering consists of asking.

It's also worth saying plainly what this project is a rehearsal for, because it is not
really the Raspberry Pi. Every project you ship for the rest of your career will have a
stakeholder who cares about outcomes and not mechanisms, a budget that forecloses the
elegant option, a teammate whose code you must both trust and verify, a tool that is
confidently wrong at the worst possible moments, a deadline that does not move, and a world
that declines to be ideal about any of it. This project is that, at one-tenth scale, with
gentler consequences and better office hours. Learning to do good work inside those
conditions, not despite them, and never while waiting for them to lift, is the transferable
skill. **The drivers and ring buffers are the vehicle. The judgment is the cargo.**

So do it the way it is designed to be done. Find a person with a problem. Build them a
machine that is awake when they are not. Use the agent as the collaborator it is (plan
first, keep the diffs small, demand evidence, merge nothing you can't explain) and write the
thinking parts yourself. Accept the constraints as the terms of the craft, and let the
limitations section tell the truth without flinching. At the end you'll have a device on a
shelf, doing a job, imperfectly and honestly, for someone who is glad it exists. Most
courses can't offer you that. This one is trying to.

---

## 20. Version History

| Version | Date | Comments |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 8/3/2026 | First public release of the assignment. |

---

## Appendix A — Sensor Starter List

> **Quick flag:** anything marked **(!)** has 5 V lurking in it somewhere, so treat those
> interfaces with a little extra respect.

Here's the thing about the Pi's GPIO pins: **they only speak 3.3 V logic, and there's zero
over-voltage protection built in.** Feed one a 5 V signal directly and it can just… die.
Silently. No warning light, no smoke, sometimes not even a clue until you notice nothing's
responding anymore. And sometimes it doesn't stop at the pin, it takes the whole SoC down
with it. That's exactly why the HC-SR04 needs a voltage divider on its echo line. The
trigger pin is fine with 5 V, but the echo pin is not, and if you wire them the same way
because "eh, they're both just signal pins," congratulations, you've found the single most
popular way to lose a Pi in Week 13.

But **power-rail mistakes are even less forgiving.** Swap VCC and GND, or let a 5 V rail
touch the 3.3 V rail while you're poking around with a multimeter, and your board usually
doesn't warn you first. It just stops working. No gradual decline, no second chances.

So here's the move: **build anything 5 V-adjacent on a breadboard first. Check your voltages
with a meter before the Pi ever gets plugged in. And always, always wire things up with the
board powered off.**

None of this is meant to be a hard boundary — think of it more as a floor. Weird, exotic
sensors are still welcome at the table, as long as the guardrails hold.

| Sensor | Interface | What it naturally teaches |
|---|---|---|
| BME280 (temp / humidity / pressure) | I2C | Multi-rate polled sampling; an approachable first target for a character driver (menu **A**) |
| DHT22 (temp / humidity) | bit-banged single-wire | Microsecond timing windows from userspace, and therefore a lesson in why kernels exist |
| HC-SR501 PIR motion | GPIO edge | Interrupts, debouncing, and the polling comparison (menu **B**) |
| HC-SR04 ultrasonic **(!)** | GPIO trigger/echo | Echo-timing jitter as a measurable scheduling artifact (menu **C**); voltage dividers |
| MPU-6050 IMU | I2C (400 kHz), FIFO | High-rate sampling without drops; ring buffers; FIFO-overflow accounting (menu **F**) |
| Photoresistor + MCP3008 | SPI ADC | SPI, and sampling an analog world on a board with no ADC |
| INMP441 microphone | I2S | Real streaming rates; DMA; buffer discipline (menu **F**) |
| Reed switch / door contact | GPIO | Events, state machines, and the cheapest ground truth you will ever get |
| MH-Z19 CO₂ | UART | Serial protocols, framing, checksums, and vendors' creative datasheets |
| Load cell + HX711 | bit-banged serial | Timing plus calibration: where systems code meets the physical world's noise |

59	## 1. Overview
60	
61	Every assignment in this course hands you a problem and asks for a program. The term
62	project reverses the polarity. It hands you a program-shaped hole in the world and asks you
63	to find it. You will design and build a working device (a Raspberry Pi, at least two
64	sensors, and software of your own) that does something a specific person actually needs
65	done. Not a demo of a sensor. Not a tutorial, reassembled. A device that could sit on a
66	shelf in that person's life and earn its electricity.
67	
68	The question that will follow you through this project, from the first memo to the final
69	defense, is this: **who wants this, and why doesn't a phone app already solve it?** The
70	second half of that question is quietly load-bearing. A phone runs its apps when someone is
71	looking at it. Your device has to be awake at 3 a.m., unattended, on the day the
72	interesting thing finally happens. Always-on, physically embedded, resource-constrained,
73	unsupervised: that's exactly the territory where processes, schedulers, interrupts,
74	storage, and IPC stop being lecture topics and start being the difference between a product
75	and a demo. You don't need to bolt operating-systems content onto this project. Choose an
76	honest problem and the operating-systems content will come to you. Uninvited, and usually
77	at inconvenient hours. The guardrails in Section 3 exist only to make sure the problem you
78	choose is honest.
79	
80	The project is deliberately open. The five concepts in Section 4 are seeds for your
81	ideation, not a menu to order from; the strongest projects most years are ideas we didn't
82	think of. What is *not* open is the standard of evidence. Your system must survive 48 hours
83	unattended and prove it with logs. Your claims about latency, throughput, and reliability
84	must be measurements, not adjectives. And at the end, each of you, separately, must be able
85	to stand in front of your own code and explain why it is the way it is. What is *not
86	expected* is perfection, and Section 5 says so at length. The world your device ships into
87	is imperfect. Your budget is finite, your sensors are cheap, and the project is graded
88	accordingly: on what you did with what you had, and on the honesty of the accounting.
89	
90	> ### Grading methodology and the demo you can't rehearse
91	>
92	> The term project accounts for **10% of your course grade** and is graded out of 100
93	> points, split the same way the assignments are: most of the points answer a question the
94	> artifacts can settle, and the rest answer a question only you can.
95	>
96	> **70 points attach to the work and its evidence:** the problem memo (5), the design
97	> document (10), the checkpoint demonstration (10), the final system with its 48-hour soak
98	> test (30), and the quantitative evaluation report (15). These are graded from things we
99	> can run, read, and re-measure.
100	>
101	> **The remaining 30 points are individual, and no teammate can earn them for you.** 10
102	> points come from the analysis of your Claude Code transcripts, on the same five-level,
103	> repository-corroborated scale used in the assignments. 20 points come from the demo-day
104	> defense: questions about lines of your own subsystems, one question from across the
105	> ownership boundary, a defense of one episode from your `PROMPTLOG.md`, and a small live
106	> modification you make to your own code, alone, at the keyboard, while we watch. So two
107	> partners can submit one flawless repository and still leave demo day with very different
108	> grades. The defense was never grading the repository. It was grading each of you.
109	>
110	> Why the split? Same reason as the assignments, scaled up. A device that works is a nice
111	> thing to have. But a pair of engineers who can each explain, unprompted, why their
112	> sampler can't drop a reading and what their watchdog does when a sensor gets unplugged?
113	> That's a nice thing to *become*, and it's the thing this course is actually for.

117	## 2. Learning Objectives
118	
119	- Translate a real user's real problem into a system design, and defend every component of
120	  that design by the problem's demands rather than by habit.
121	- Build an embedded sensing product on Linux that exercises at least two
122	  below-the-application-layer mechanisms: device drivers, interrupt handling, real-time
123	  scheduling, custom storage, or multi-process architectures with fault isolation.
124	- Write the product's intelligence yourself (statistics, signal processing, state machines,
125	  control) and know precisely why a threshold wouldn't have sufficed.

127	  stability over days rather than seconds, and graceful degradation when hardware

130	  present latency, utilization, and reliability numbers you can stand behind under

133	  development process (Claude Code included) that leaves a verifiable trail.

148	## 3. The Guardrails: What "Non-Trivial" Means Here
149	
150	An open-ended project needs a floor, or the path of least resistance becomes a Python
151	script that polls a sensor and prints a number. Five guardrails define the floor.
152	Everything above them is yours.
153	
154	### 3.1 Two sensors that cooperate
155	
156	Your device must incorporate **at least two physically distinct sensors**, and they must
157	**cooperate**: fused into one decision, correlated against each other, or feeding a single
158	shared pipeline whose behavior depends on both. Two independent demos stapled together at
159	the README do not satisfy this requirement. That's one sensor short of the assignment,
160	twice. Cooperation is also where the systems content hides. Two sensors almost never want
161	the same sampling rate, the same interface, or the same latency budget, and reconciling
162	those differences inside one program is the first real design problem this project hands
163	you.
164	
165	### 3.2 Below the application layer: the mechanism menu
166	
167	Your system must include **at least two** of the following mechanisms, implemented by you,
168	identified explicitly in your design document, and measured in your evaluation. This is the
169	guardrail that keeps the project an operating-systems project rather than a wiring
170	exercise.
171	
172	| # | Mechanism | What "measured" means |
173	|---|---|---|
174	| **A** | A kernel module or character driver for one of your sensors, exposing it via `/dev` or sysfs | Correct concurrent access; behavior under load; a clean `dmesg` |
175	| **B** | Interrupt-driven input, with a head-to-head comparison against a polling design | Event latency distribution and CPU utilization, both ways |
176	| **C** | Real-time scheduling (`SCHED_FIFO`/`SCHED_RR`) for a latency-critical path | Jitter and deadline-miss rate vs. the default scheduler, under load |
177	| **D** | A custom storage layer: ring buffer, append-only log, or small FUSE filesystem, with an explicit crash-consistency story | Write batching and `fsync` discipline; recovery after a mid-write power cut |
178	| **E** | A multi-process architecture: sensors isolated in separate processes, a hub aggregating over IPC (shared memory, message queues, or Unix domain sockets), a supervisor that survives any child dying | Kill any child at any time; the system degrades, logs, recovers |
179	| **F** | A high-rate sampling pipeline with a no-drop guarantee: lock-free or single-producer/single-consumer ring between capture and consumption | Sustained rate with zero drops, proven by sequence accounting, under CPU contention |
180	
181	Choose the two (or more) that **your problem demands**, not the two that look easiest. The
182	design document (Section 8) requires you to justify each choice from the user's
183	requirements, and the defense will test that justification. Figure 1 shows where these
184	mechanisms live in a reference architecture.
185	
186	### Figure 1 — A reference architecture, not a required one
187	
188	```
189	  sampler daemon        storage layer (D)        analysis engine              interface
190	  SCHED_FIFO (C),  shm  ring / append log,  mmap  your statistics,      UDS    CLI / LAN
191	  no-drop ring (F) ring crash-consistent    / mq  DSP, state machines  ─────▶  dashboard
192	
193	────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── kernel/user boundary ──
194	
195	  kernel space:  I2C / GPIO subsystems · your character driver (A) · IRQ handling (B)
196	
197	                                                                       supervisor /
198	                                                                       watchdog (E)
199	                                                              ▲ restart on hang or crash
200	
201	        Sensor A              Sensor B                Actuator
202	       I2C, 10 Hz         GPIO, event-driven         (optional)
203	```
204	
205	*Letters mark where the Section 3.2 menu mechanisms live; pick at least two, driven by your
206	problem.*
207	
208	Sensors enter through the kernel; a sampler moves data into a storage layer without losing
209	any; an analysis engine you wrote turns data into decisions; an interface lets a human see
210	them; a supervisor keeps the whole thing alive at 3 a.m. Your product may collapse, split,
211	or rearrange these boxes freely. The graded requirement is only that **at least two menu
212	mechanisms exist somewhere in it, below the application layer, written by you.**
213	
214	### 3.3 The intelligence is yours
215	
216	The running product **may not call a hosted model of any kind** (no Claude, no other LLM,
217	no cloud inference API) and **may not embed a pretrained model** unless you petition for it
218	in your design document and receive approval. All analysis, detection, diagnosis, and
219	decision logic must be code you wrote: rolling statistics, spectral features, sensor-fusion
220	rules, state machines, control loops. Libraries for mathematical primitives (an FFT, a
221	linear solver) are fine, provided you can explain what the primitive computes and why your
222	pipeline needs it.
223	
224	Two rules of thumb bound the requirement, one from below and one from above:
225	
226	- **From below:** if a single threshold could do it, it isn't intelligence, and your product
227	  must do something with its two sensors that an `if`-statement could not.

262	practice rooms, bee hives: the world is oversupplied with small, real problems that a phone
263	app can't solve because a phone is never there when it matters. Find one. Every design
264	decision you'll be asked to defend gets easier to defend when the answer can begin with
265	"because the user needs…".

269	## 4. Ideation
270	
271	This is where the project actually begins, so it gets more room than any other section. I
272	am including 5 worked seeds. But they are **seeds, not a menu**: none is required, all are
273	claimable by any team, and the strongest proposals most years are ideas we didn't think of.
274	Read the seeds less for their subjects than for their skeleton. Every one of them has the
275	same bones: an absent observer, an always-on device, intelligence a threshold couldn't
276	provide, and a user you could name. Your job is to find a problem with the same skeleton
277	and a different flesh.
278	
279	### 4.1 Three ways to find your own
280	
281	**Audit a week.** Carry a note for one week and write down every time you, or someone
282	near/close-to you, utters one of two sentences: *"I wish I knew…"* and *"by the time I
283	noticed…"*. These are sensor products wearing plain clothes. The first names a measurement
284	that is absent. The second names a measurement that existed but had nobody watching it,
285	which is the 3 a.m. test passing itself, unprompted, in ordinary conversation. A week of
286	honest auditing typically yields a dozen candidates, of which two survive the guardrails.
287	And that's exactly as many as you need.
288	
289	**Shrink an industry.** Predictive maintenance, cold-chain monitoring, occupancy analytics,
290	precision agriculture, structural health monitoring: entire companies exist to do each of
291	these at scale, which means someone has already established, expensively, that the problem
292	is worth solving. Take one. Shrink it to a single machine, a single room, a single shelf,
293	and you inherit a validated problem sized for a semester. You also inherit something rarer:
294	the discovery, which tends to stay with people, that the distance between a course project
295	and a real industry is mostly a matter of scale, not of kind.
296	
297	**Instrument a devotion.** Hobbies are problems folks have volunteered for: fermentation,
298	aquariums, climbing training, beekeeping, film-developing chemistry, model rocketry.
299	Devotees make the best users, for three reasons that matter to your grade. They already
300	measure things by hand, so the value of automating the measurement is pre-established. They
301	will actually run your device. And they will tell you (at length and for free) exactly what
302	it gets wrong, which is the most expensive kind of feedback in all of engineering; that is
303	now available here for the price of listening.
304	
305	Whatever you find, run it through the guardrails of Section 3 as filters, and through
306	Section 5 as a reality check. Ideally before the memo. Certainly before the design document.
307	
308	### 4.2 Seed 1: "Is my elderly parent okay today?" (ambient wellness monitor)
309	
310	The user is an adult child who lives an hour, or a continent, away from a parent who lives
311	alone. The moment the product exists for is a quiet one: not the fall, but the morning that
312	didn't follow its rhythm, noticed hours before anyone would have been frightened enough to
313	call. Every existing answer asks the parent to *do* something. Wear the pendant. Charge the
314	watch. Answer the daily check-in. And the failure mode is that the people most at risk are
315	precisely the people least likely to keep doing it. The design brief is then a device that
316	demands nothing: no camera, no microphone, no button, no new habit. That restraint is not a
317	limitation to apologize for. It's the product's spine, and a memo that can articulate why a
318	motion sensor is more respectful than a camera is a memo that understands its user.
319	
320	**Engineering:** a PIR motion sensor and a door or pressure sensor, learning a household's
321	rhythm. The intelligence (all of it yours) is per-hour activity histograms over a rolling
322	window of weeks, a deviation score that knows a Tuesday from a Sunday, and alert hysteresis.
323	Because the real analytical problem here isn't detection. It's restraint. A monitor that
324	cries wolf twice gets unplugged. An unplugged monitor is worse than none, because somebody
325	far away believes it's on duty. Natural mechanisms: **E**, because a silently dead wellness
326	monitor is this product's own nightmare scenario, which makes process isolation and
327	supervision requirements rather than garnish; and **D**, because weeks of learned baseline
328	must survive a power cut. A scoped-down version that still clears every bar: one room, one
329	rhythm, two weeks of baseline, and an alert log you evaluate for false-alarm rate. No paging
330	infrastructure required.
331	
332	### 4.3 Seed 2: "Why does my sourdough / homebrew / greenhouse keep failing?" (environmental coach)
333	
334	The user is a devotee (Section 4.1, third method) whose batches keep dying and who has
335	already tried the obvious: a thermometer that's glanced at while awake. The insight the
336	product is built on is that what kills the batch is almost never the moment anyone is
337	looking. It's the 4 a.m. excursion. The slow weekend drift. The heater that quietly began
338	short-cycling on Tuesday. And the user's real question is never "what is the temperature?";
339	it's "what is wrong?" The distance between those two questions, between a reading and a
340	diagnosis, is exactly the distance your intelligence has to cover. No threshold covers it.
341	
342	**Engineering:** temperature/humidity plus light or CO₂, sampled at rates that differ by an
343	order of magnitude, flowing through a storage layer of your own design (**D**), often behind
344	a no-drop pipeline (**F**). The intelligence is rolling statistics, rate-of-change
345	detection, and, the satisfying part, *signature detection*. A short-cycling heater
346	oscillates with a period and amplitude you can measure. A failing seal shows up as indoor
347	humidity coupling to the outdoor weather. A dying yeast culture flattens a CO₂ curve that
348	should be climbing. Encoding that physics into diagnostic rules requires actually learning
349	the domain. Which means talking to your user, which is the job. **Where it bites:** the
350	temptation to promise twelve diagnoses and deliver them all vaguely. Three diagnoses, each
351	with a measured true- and false-positive rate against failure episodes you provoked on
352	purpose, is the far stronger project. And Section 5 is about why provoking them on purpose
353	is not a workaround but a method.
354	
355	### 4.4 Seed 3: "Did something happen while I was gone?" (explainable security node)
356	
357	Everyone with a door has asked the question. The commercial answer is four hours of footage
358	nobody will ever watch. This product's differentiator is one word: **explainable**. It
359	answers with a timeline (*3:12 p.m., something person-sized, eleven seconds, moving away*)
360	that a human can read in five seconds and interrogate afterward. The user is anyone who
361	wants that answer without becoming a security-camera hobbyist and, not incidentally,
362	without pointing an internet-connected lens at their own life. Like Seed 1, the absence of a
363	camera is a feature you can defend out loud.
364	
365	**Engineering:** PIR motion plus ultrasonic ranging in an interrupt-driven pipeline. That's
366	mechanism **B**, with the polling comparison built into your evaluation, and usually **C**,
367	because ranging an object during a two-second event is a latency budget you have to actually
368	meet rather than merely admire. The intelligence is fusion (*motion says something, range
369	says how big and how far*), debouncing, event segmentation, and the design of the timeline
370	itself. A log schema from which a human can reconstruct the truth is a genuine engineering
371	artifact, and it's the thing your demo-day answer to "was that the cat?" will be read from.
372	Speaking of the cat: it is this seed's honest adversary, and a magnetic reed switch on the
373	door is the cheapest ground-truth generator you will ever wire. Every real entry gets a free
374	label. **Scoped-down version:** three event classes (person-sized, small, unknown)
375	classified honestly, with the confusion matrix to prove it, beats ten classes classified
376	wishfully.
377	
378	### 4.5 Seed 4: "Is this machine about to break?" (small-shop predictive maintenance)
379	
380	There is an entire industry (vibration analysis, condition monitoring) built on the fact
381	that machines announce their failures early, in frequencies, to anyone equipped to listen.
382	Its instruments cost more than your car. Its customers are factories. The user here is
383	everyone below that line: the shop with one compressor, the makerspace with one 3-D printer,
384	the laundromat, the house with a furnace fan. The moment the product exists for is the new
385	noise that started on a Tuesday when nobody was in the room. We tend to light up on
386	discovering that the hobby-scale version of a real industry fits inside one semester and
387	about $18 in parts. That discovery is worth having. And nothing says it has to expire with
388	the course.
389	
390	**Engineering:** an accelerometer (the MPU-6050's hardware FIFO is your friend) and a
391	temperature sensor. Mechanism **F** is nearly mandatory, because a dropped sample corrupts
392	the spectrum; this is the seed where the systems work and the analysis work hold each other
393	honest most tightly. **C** is close behind, and **A** is there for the ambitious. The
394	intelligence is feature extraction (FFT band energies, RMS trends) compared against a
395	healthy baseline you recorded yourself. **Where it bites, instructively:** you can't wait a
396	semester for a real bearing to fail. So you induce faults. Tape a washer to a fan blade for
397	imbalance. Loosen a mounting bolt. Run the printer with a dry rod. Record labeled captures
398	of each. That's not cheating; it's how the real industry builds its test sets, and Section 5
399	makes it doctrine. The scoped-down version is also simply the honest one: *"detects the
400	three faults I can induce on this machine, with these error rates"* survives a defense.
401	*"Predicts failure"* does not.
402	
403	### 4.6 Seed 5: "Ask the room" (facilities query hub)
404	
405	The user is whoever answers for a room that other people complain about: the practice-space
406	manager, the lab steward, the roommate whose name is on the lease. The complaints arrive in
407	the past tense. *"It was freezing in here yesterday morning."* *"It gets stuffy every
408	afternoon."* And no live dashboard on earth answers a past-tense question. The product is a
409	**memory for a building**: several sensors, a history, and an interface that can answer
410	"mean CO₂ by hour, weekdays, last month" in less time than the argument takes.
411	
412	**Engineering:** three or more sensors (air quality, sound level, temperature) as isolated
413	processes feeding a hub over IPC. That's mechanism **E**, with real supervision, since a
414	facilities record with a three-day hole has lost the argument it exists to win. Everything
415	persists through a storage layer (**D**) whose retention, rollup, and `fsync` policies you
416	must actually decide rather than inherit. The intelligence is the query engine: time-range
417	selection, aggregation, alignment of multi-rate series, and cross-sensor correlation
418	(afternoon CO₂ tracking the sound level is an occupancy story told by two sensors that never
419	met). **Where it bites:** interface ambition. Resist the pretty web app. A crisp CLI with
420	five query verbs and exact semantics is more defensible, and far more extensible at the
421	live-modification station on demo day, than a dashboard with none. This is the seed for
422	teams who suspect they might enjoy building databases, because it is one, in miniature,
423	standing on an IPC layer they also built.

427	## 5. Building in an Imperfect World
428	
429	Somewhere between the memo and the checkpoint, every team hits the same wall. It's worth
430	telling you now that **the wall is scheduled.** The sensor your design really wants is a
431	$400 thermal imager and your budget is $60. The $4 accelerometer you bought instead has a
432	noise floor sitting exactly where the interesting signal lives. The CO₂ sensor needs three
433	minutes to warm up and drifts with the weather. And the data you need at the scale you want
434	(a year of failing compressors, a winter of greenhouse nights, 104 labeled door events) does
435	not exist, can't be bought, and won't be gathered in one semester by one device on one
436	shelf. None of this means you chose the wrong project! It means the project has become real.
437	Engineering has been called the art of the possible. The phrase is not a consolation; it's
438	the job description. **The constraints are not in the way of the work. They are the medium
439	the work is done in.**
440	
441	The unproductive response is to stare at what can't be done. The productive one is to ask,
442	repeatedly and in roughly this order, what can:
443	
444	- **Substitute.** Downgrade the sensor; keep the problem. A PIR and a door switch see more
445	  of a household's rhythm than you'd guess a thermal camera was needed for. A microphone's
446	  RMS level is a serviceable occupancy proxy. And two cheap sensors that corroborate each
447	  other routinely outperform one expensive one standing alone. Notice that "corroborate each
448	  other" is Section 3.1 arriving early, wearing a budget. Record in the design document what
449	  you wanted, what you used, and what the substitution costs in capability.
450	
451	- **Make your own ground truth.** You can't wait for the bearing to fail, so you provoke the
452	  conditions and label the recordings: the taped washer, the loosened bolt, the greenhouse
453	  vent propped open on purpose, a one-week paper logbook of real door events. **Ten labeled
454	  recordings you made are worth more than ten thousand unlabeled samples you found**,
455	  because you know what yours mean. And at the defense, you will be asked how you know.
456	
457	- **Replay.** Build a harness that feeds recorded sensor streams through your real pipeline
458	  at real or accelerated speed. Now a month of "operation" fits in an afternoon, rare events
459	  can be rehearsed on demand, and regressions are caught by re-running last week. The
460	  harness is not a workaround to be embarrassed about. It's a legitimate systems artifact
461	  (real products are tested exactly this way), and building one that faithfully preserves
462	  inter-sample timing is engineering in its own right. **One rule, absolute: replayed or
463	  synthesized data is labeled as such everywhere it appears. In logs. In the report. In the
464	  demo. The 48-hour soak and the live demonstration run on live sensors; everything else may
465	  run on honest replay.**
466	
467	- **Narrow the claim.** Shrink the sentence until it is true. *"Detects the three faults I
468	  can induce on this compressor, with these error rates"* is a claim that survives
469	  cross-examination; *"predicts failure"* is not. A narrow claim, met and measured,
470	  outscores a broad claim that's gestured at. On this rubric, and on every rubric that
471	  matters after this course.
472	
473	What this means for your grade deserves to be said without hedging: **the term project does
474	not expect a perfect project. It expects an honest one that works.** We grade your reasoning
475	about constraints, never the absence of constraints, because the absence of constraints is
476	not a condition that occurs in nature. The design document has a home for this reasoning
477	(Section 8), and the evaluation report's limitations section is where it pays off. The team
478	that writes *"we wanted X, we could afford Y, and here is precisely what Y cost us"* has
479	demonstrated the exact judgment this course exists to build, and will be graded like it. The
480	team that quietly papers over the gap has converted an ordinary constraint (the most
481	ordinary thing in engineering) into an integrity problem. And that is the worst trade
482	available anywhere in this course. We live in an imperfect world. Every system you will ever
483	ship will ship into it. So you may as well learn to do it well, and without apology, now.

608	### 10.1 What changes in a team of two
609	
610	- **One `CLAUDE.md`, two authors.** The file is team law: build and deploy commands, the
611	  hard constraints (no runtime model calls; no network dependence; every daemon
612	  supervisable), style rules, and the ownership map. Both partners maintain it. The agent
613	  reads it in every session, so a constraint that lives only in one partner's head protects
614	  nothing. A sample is in [Appendix B](#appendix-b--sample-team-claudemd).
615	- **Sessions are personal.** Each partner works in their own clone and their own Claude Code
616	  sessions, and submits their own transcripts. Your 10 process points are computed from
617	  *your* `.jsonl` files, corroborated against *your* commits.
618	- **Your partner is a reviewer the agent can't replace.** Every milestone's diffs get two
619	  reviews: a fresh-context agent review (Assignment 0, Step 7) and a human one by the
620	  partner who did not write the code. Each partner's `PROMPTLOG.md` must include at least
621	  one episode of reviewing the other's work: what you questioned, what the answer was, what
622	  changed. *A team whose two halves never disagreed about anything all semester has not been
623	  reviewing.*
624	- **Commits carry names.** At least **40 meaningful commits** across the project, with both
625	  partners well represented. A history in which one partner authored under a quarter of the
626	  substantive commits will be probed hard at the individual defense. Which, remember, is 20
627	  individual points.
628	
629	### 10.2 What changes when the target is hardware
630	
631	The agent can't see your breadboard and this cuts both ways. It will confidently reason
632	about a sensor it has never met, and it will be wrong in ways that only an instrument can
633	catch. So the evidence discipline of Assignment 0, Step 5 gets a hardware clause: **close
634	the loop with measurements.** Paste `dmesg` verbatim. Paste the timing capture. Paste
635	`/proc/interrupts` before and after. The agent reads a kernel oops better than a vague
636	description of one. And so will you, by the end of this project.
637	
638	> Our DHT22 reads fail checksum roughly 30% of the time, but only when the analysis process
639	> is busy. Here is the pulse-width capture from the logic analyzer for one failed read:
640	> `[paste]`. Our read path bit-bangs from userspace via libgpiod. Identify where the timing
641	> budget breaks under scheduling delay, and propose two designs that survive it, with
642	> tradeoffs, before writing any code.
643	
644	### 10.3 What changes because the model is banned from the product
645	
646	Nothing about how you develop; everything about what you ship. Use the agent freely to plan
647	the supervisor, explain `epoll`, draft the FFT feature extractor, and generate labeled test
648	fixtures for your detector. But the shipped tree must honor Section 3.3, and **the boundary
649	must be legible: a grader reading your repository should be able to confirm in one minute
650	that the product's only network activity is its own LAN interface.** And if you're ever
651	tempted to resolve a hard analysis problem by "just asking a model" at runtime, notice that
652	the temptation *is* the assignment. The hard analysis problem is the part you are here to
653	learn to solve.
654	
655	### 10.4 Prompt patterns: good vs. useless
656	
657	| Useless | Effective |
658	|---|---|
659	| "make the sensor work" | "`i2cdetect` sees the BME280 at 0x76 but our reads return 0x80 in every field. Here is our init sequence and the datasheet's required mode transition [paste both]. Diff them and identify the missing step; do not rewrite the module." |
660	| "fix the crash" | "`dmesg` oops attached [paste]. The fault is in our driver's read path, which takes lock at line 84. Walk the call path from IRQ context and identify what we are doing there that IRQ context forbids." |
661	| "make it faster" | "`perf report`: 38% of sampler CPU in `memcpy`. Plan a zero-copy handoff from the capture ring to the consumer given single-producer/single-consumer and a 16 KiB budget. Risks and invariants first; no code." |
662	| "write the daemon" | "Plan the supervisor: restart policy with backoff, fd hygiene across fork/exec, and how we avoid a restart storm when a sensor is physically unplugged rather than crashed. List what you'd log at each decision." |
663	| "why is the soak failing" | "RSS grew 40 MB over 12 hours; hourly heartbeats attached. Rank hypotheses by likelihood given that event counts are flat but query counts are not, then propose the cheapest instrumentation to discriminate between the top two." |
664	
665	**Transcript submission.** Identical to Assignment 0, per partner: the raw `.jsonl` session
666	files from `~/.claude/projects/`, copied in as-is. Not summarized. Not exported. Not
667	retyped. Work in a dedicated project directory per partner so the copy is one `cp`.
668	Transcripts are purged locally after 30 days by default, and this project spans more than 30
669	days, so copy them out at every milestone or raise `cleanupPeriodDays` now. **Losing Week-5
670	transcripts to the default in Week-15 is a foreseeable loss; foreseeable losses are not
671	excused.**

675	## 11. Personalized Verification: Demo Day
676	
677	Every team demos live; every student defends individually. The session runs roughly thirty
678	minutes per team, in 3 movements.
679	
680	**The demonstration.** Your device, running your soaked build, doing its job. At a moment of
681	our choosing, **we will inject a fault, most often by unplugging one of your sensors
682	mid-demo.** This is announced now so that nobody can call it unfair later. The graded
683	behaviors are graceful degradation, honest reporting through your own interface, and the log
684	line proving the system noticed. A device that freezes, lies, or crashes when hardware
685	misbehaves has failed its user at exactly the moment it existed for.
686	
687	**The individual defense.** Separately, each partner answers for their own subsystems: lines
688	of your code (*"what wakes this thread?"*, *"what happens to this fd when the child dies?"*,
689	*"why can't this ring overwrite an unread sample?"*), one judgment call from your
690	`PROMPTLOG.md`, and one question from across the ownership boundary. Because owning your
691	half deeply does not excuse understanding the other half not at all.
692	
693	**The live modification.** Each partner, alone at the keyboard, makes one small
694	previously-unseen change to their own subsystem, starting from the submitted source: a new
695	field in the heartbeat, a changed threshold semantic, a new flag on the query CLI. Small for
696	an author. Revealing for anyone else.
697	
698	**Why this exists.** For the same reason it exists in the assignments, with the stakes
699	raised. A repository, a report, and a beautiful demo video can all be produced without
700	understanding. Thirty minutes of your own code behaving unexpectedly in front of you cannot.
701	The defense is not an audit bolted onto the project; it's the project's final measurement,
702	and the quantity it measures is *you*.

709

711	  `README.md` that takes a TA from a clean Pi to your running system without your help. *If
712	  the TA can't boot it, the TA can't grade it.*

714	  began, with a short changelog of what M2's version got wrong), and `EVALUATION.md`.
715	- **Soak evidence:** the raw, unedited logs of the 48-hour run, including the injected fault.
716	- **`CLAUDE.md`**, checked in and evolving across the milestones.
717	- **Per partner:** `PROMPTLOG.md` (6–10 annotated episodes, including one revised plan, one
718	  rejected diff, one tool-output debugging loop with real hardware evidence, and one review
719	  of your partner's work), `REFLECTION.md` (one page: where the agent was most and least
720	  reliable against real hardware; one bug it introduced that you caught, and how), and the
721	  raw `.jsonl` transcripts.

746	die has not passed the soak. It has outrun it.* Second, the transcript scale is applied per
747	partner, to that partner's own sessions. Working in one shared login defeats this and will
